335	**[XVIII. REOPENER PROVISIONS]{.underline}**
336	
337	**18.1** *General Reopener.* The State may reopen this Consent Decree and require GRS to perform additional work, provide additional financial assurance, pay additional penalties, or take such other actions as the State deems appropriate, if any of the following conditions is found to exist:
338	
339	> \(a\) Previously unknown contamination is discovered at or emanating from the Facility, whether in soil, groundwater, surface water, sediment, air, or any other environmental medium;
340	>
341	> \(b\) Information not available at the time of entry of this Consent Decree reveals that the contamination addressed by this Consent Decree is of a greater magnitude, extent, duration, or concentration than was indicated in the Remedial Investigation or was otherwise previously known to the Parties;
342	>
343	> \(c\) The selected remedy at any SWMU or AOC fails to achieve compliance with applicable Remediation Objectives or Class I groundwater quality standards within the timeframes established in this Consent Decree, or fails to adequately protect human health or the environment.
344	
345	**18.2** *No Limitation.* There shall be no temporal limitation on the State\'s right to reopen this Consent Decree under this Section. The State may exercise its reopener rights at any time, including after the completion of corrective action, the attainment of Remediation Objectives, or the expiration of the monitoring period established under Section XII. The reopener provisions of this Section shall survive the termination of this Consent Decree and shall remain in full force and effect in perpetuity.
346	
347	**18.3** *Procedure.* The State shall provide GRS with written notice of its intent to reopen this Consent Decree, specifying the factual and legal basis for reopening and the additional actions the State believes are required. GRS shall have thirty (30) days from receipt of such notice to respond in writing. If the Parties are unable to agree on the scope of additional work or other actions required, the State may petition the Court to modify this Consent Decree to incorporate such additional requirements as the Court deems appropriate. The Court shall grant the State\'s petition unless GRS demonstrates, by clear and convincing evidence, that the reopener is not warranted.
348	
349	**18.4** *FRC Reopener.* FRC shall have the right to petition the Court to reopen this Consent Decree on the same grounds and under the same procedures as the State, as set forth in Sections 18.1 through 18.3 above. FRC\'s reopener rights under this Section shall be coextensive with the State\'s reopener rights and shall be subject to the same conditions and procedures.
350	
351	**[XIX. TERMINATION]{.underline}**
352	
353	**19.1** *Conditions for Termination.* This Consent Decree may be terminated upon the joint motion of all Parties, or upon motion by GRS with the consent of the State and FRC, after GRS has demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Court that each of the following conditions has been met:
354	
355	> \(a\) GRS has paid all civil penalties required under Section VI, all stipulated penalties accrued under Section IX, and all FRC payments required under Section X, in full and without offset or deduction;
356	>
357	> \(b\) GRS has completed all corrective action required under Section VII and has achieved and maintained compliance with all applicable Remediation Objectives and Class I groundwater quality standards at all SWMUs and AOCs identified in the Remedial Investigation;
358	>
359	> \(c\) GRS has completed all thirty (30) years of groundwater monitoring required under Section XII, including the submission of all required monitoring reports;
360	>
361	> \(d\) GRS has fully funded the SEP required under Section VIII and the SEP has been completed by FRC in accordance with Section 8.5;
362	>
363	> \(e\) GRS has satisfied all other obligations under this Consent Decree, including but not limited to the maintenance of financial assurance, the submission of all required reports, and compliance with all access and information requirements.
364	
365	**19.2** *Opposition.* The State or FRC may oppose any motion by GRS to terminate this Consent Decree, and the Court shall consider such opposition before ruling on the motion. The Court may deny a motion to terminate if it finds that GRS has not fully satisfied all conditions for termination set forth in Section 19.1, or if it finds that termination would not be in the public interest.
366	
367	**19.3** *Survival.* The reopener provisions of Section XVIII shall survive the termination of this Consent Decree and shall remain in full force and effect following such termination. The record-keeping obligations of Section 13.1 and the privilege waiver of Section 14.2 shall likewise survive termination of this Consent Decree for the periods specified therein.

412	
413	**21.1** *Entire Agreement.* This Consent Decree, including all Appendices hereto, constitutes the entire agreement among the Parties with respect to the subject matter hereof and supersedes all prior and contemporaneous negotiations, representations, warranties, understandings, and agreements, whether written or oral, relating to the subject matter of this Consent Decree. 414	
415	**21.2** *Modifications.* This Consent Decree may be modified only by a written agreement signed by all Parties and approved by the Court, except that non-material modifications to schedules and deadlines (not to exceed sixty (60) days) may be made by written agreement between GRS and Illinois EPA without Court approval. Any modification that extends a deadline by more than sixty (60) days, modifies the substantive obligations of any Party, or changes the amount of any penalty, payment, or financial assurance requirement shall require Court approval. FRC shall be notified of all proposed modifications, whether material or non-material.
416	
417	**21.3** *Severability.* If any provision of this Consent Decree is held to be invalid, illegal, or unenforceable by a court of competent jurisdiction, the validity, legality, and enforceability of the remaining provisions shall not in any way be affected or impaired thereby, and the invalid provision shall be modified to the minimum extent necessary to make it valid and enforceable while preserving the intent of the Parties.
418	
419	**21.4** *Governing Law.* This Consent Decree shall be governed by, and construed and interpreted in accordance with, the laws of the State of Illinois, without regard to its conflict-of-laws principles. To the extent that any issue arising under this Consent Decree involves the interpretation of federal law, including RCRA, 42 U.S.C. §§ 6901 *et seq.*, such issue shall be resolved in accordance with applicable federal law.
420	
421	**21.5** *Counterparts.* This Consent Decree may be executed in two or more counterparts, each of which shall be deemed an original, and all of which together shall constitute one and the same instrument. Facsimile and electronic signatures shall be deemed to have the same legal effect as original signatures.
422	
423	**21.6** *Headings.* The section headings and captions used in this Consent Decree are inserted for convenience of reference only and shall not affect the meaning, interpretation, or construction of any provision of this Consent Decree.
424

The State shall publish notice of the proposed Consent Decree and the opportunity for public comment in a newspaper of general circulation in Winnebago County and on the Illinois Attorney General\'s website. The State shall respond to any significant comments received during the public comment period and shall file a response to comments with the Court prior to requesting entry of the Decree.
426	
427	**21.8** *No Waiver.* The failure of any Party to enforce any provision of this Consent Decree, or to exercise any right or remedy available hereunder, shall not constitute a waiver of such provision, right, or remedy, and shall not limit or impair the right of any Party to enforce such provision or exercise such right or remedy at any later time. No waiver of any provision of this Consent Decree shall be effective unless made in writing and signed by the waiving Party.

Neither the State nor FRC shall bear any cost or expense arising from GRS\'s obligations under this Consent Decree.

content.content:
From : "Rachel A. Downing" <rdowning@hbl-law.com>
To : "Kevin M. Pratt" <kpratt@hbl-law.com>
Date : Wed, 18 Sep 2024 09:47:00 -0000
Subject : Re: GRS Consent Decree Markup — Strategy and Priorities [PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT]
Content-Type : text/plain; charset="utf-8"
Content-Transfer-Encoding : quoted-printable
MIME-Version : 1.0
Kevin —

I got off a call yesterday afternoon with Sandra Frey and Tom Ellison to discuss the proposed Consent Decree that Calloway's office circulated on September 8. I want to download while it's fresh and give you clear direction on the markup.

Bottom line: GRS wants to settle. This case has been hanging over them since April 2021 (Case No. 2021-CH-00847), and neither Tom nor Sandra has any appetite to litigate this before Judge Sung. But the decree as drafted has several provisions that are either operationally unworkable or fundamentally unfair, and we need to push back hard on those while keeping the overall deal intact.

Calloway's deadline for returning the markup is October 7, 2024. I need your first draft of the redline and an accompanying cover memo on my desk by September 30 so we have a full week to refine before we send it out.

One critical point before I get into the specifics: **this is NOT a wholesale rewrite.** Calloway's team will toss it in the trash if we redline every sentence. We need to pick our battles strategically. I've organized the issues below in priority order.

---

**1. THE LIQUIDITY PROBLEM — TOP PRIORITY**

Tom was emphatic on the call: the financial assurance requirement and the penalty payment schedule as drafted are simply not feasible. This isn't a negotiating posture — it's a hard financial constraint. Let me walk through the numbers.

The proposed decree requires:

- **$1.5 million civil penalty** payable within 30 days of entry.
- **$16.2 million in financial assurance** (Section 7.3 — 150% of the $10.8 million estimated remediation cost) posted within 60 days of entry.
- **Combined near-term cash demand: $17.7 million.**

GRS's revolving credit facility with Beacon Commercial Bank is $40 million, but $27.3 million is currently drawn. That leaves $12.7 million in available capacity. So we're looking at a $17.7 million demand against $12.7 million in available credit — a $5 million gap. Sandra confirmed on the call that GRS cannot increase the facility or obtain additional credit in the near term. And before you ask — the Pinnacle Indemnity Group environmental policy ($5M limit, $500K SIR) won't help. It has a known-conditions exclusion predating the April 1, 2019 policy inception, and Illinois EPA's violations were first identified in the March 2020 inspection. That policy is effectively worthless for this exposure.

To be clear, GRS is a healthy company — 2023 EBITDA was approximately $22.5 million. The problem is cash flow and credit availability in the near term, not solvency.

Here's what I want you to do:

*On financial assurance:* Propose reducing the multiplier from 150% to 120% of estimated remediation costs. At 120%, the requirement drops to $12.96 million, which is tight but within the remaining capacity on the Beacon facility. I've seen 120% far more often than 150% in Illinois consent decrees — 150% is aggressive and we should say so. Also propose extending the posting deadline from 60 days to 120 days to give GRS time to arrange the instruments. And the decree should expressly allow alternative financial assurance mechanisms — corporate guarantee, financial test, or demonstration of financial capability under 35 IAC 725 Subpart H (the Illinois analog to 40 CFR 264.143). The AG may push back on the corporate guarantee, but we should at least get the financial test option in there.

*On penalty payment schedule:* Propose extending the initial $1.5 million payment from 30 days to 90 days of entry. Also consider whether the financial assurance posting can be staggered — e.g., 50% within 120 days, balance within 180 days. This is a negotiating position and we may not get all of it, but we need breathing room.

Kevin, I cannot overstate this: **the financial assurance and liquidity issues are non-negotiable.** If the decree as drafted forces GRS into a covenant default on the Beacon facility, the whole settlement falls apart. Frame this in the markup as a practical feasibility issue, not a preference. We're not saying we don't want to post assurance — we're saying the decree as written makes it mathematically impossible in the specified timeframe.

---

**2. THE ILLUSORY COVENANT NOT TO SUE**

This is the second-biggest problem in the decree and, candidly, the one that bothers me the most as a matter of principle.

Look at Section 16.1. As drafted, neither the State nor FRC covenants not to sue until GRS has (a) achieved all remediation standards at all SWMUs and AOCs AND (b) completed the full 30-year monitoring program. Think about what that means: GRS gets zero litigation peace for potentially 25 to 35 years after entry. That's not a covenant — it's a promissory note that never comes due.

The whole point of a consent decree settlement is that both sides get something. GRS is paying $3.75 million in penalties, $2.0 million for the SEP, $600,000 to FRC, and spending $10.8 million-plus on remediation. In exchange, the company should receive meaningful finality.

Here's what I want you to propose — a **phased covenant structure**:

- **Upon entry of the Consent Decree:** The State and FRC covenant not to sue on all civil penalty claims arising from the violations alleged in the Complaint. The penalty component is settled immediately and finally.
- **Upon Illinois EPA certification that the selected remedy has been implemented and remediation standards have been achieved** (the "Remedy Completion" milestone): The State and FRC covenant not to sue on injunctive relief claims — i.e., no further corrective action demands beyond what's in the decree, subject to the reopener.
- **Monitoring obligations survive independently** and are not a precondition to the covenant.

Also propose that the covenant include contribution protection under both CERCLA § 113(f)(2) and applicable Illinois law, so GRS is not exposed to third-party claims seeking to shift liability for the contamination addressed by the decree.

This is a **high priority negotiating position**. I fully expect Calloway to push back, but the current formulation is indefensible. There is room to compromise on the exact trigger points, but GRS must get a meaningful covenant at some point prior to the end of 30 years of monitoring. If we can't move the AG on this, Tom may walk, and I wouldn't blame him.

---

**3. THE CONSOLIDATED METALWORKS / SWMU-4 PROBLEM**

You know the background here, but let me frame the issue in light of the Terravance RI Summary Memorandum (the draft submitted January 15, 2023) and the recent supplemental analysis from Dr. Sheffield.

SWMU-4 (Landfill Cell B) shows vinyl chloride at 3.8 µg/L in monitoring well MW-12 versus the Class I groundwater standard of 2.0 µg/L under 35 IAC 620.410. The proposed decree holds GRS solely responsible for SWMU-4 remediation, estimated at $1.9 million. But Terravance's analysis indicates the vinyl chloride may be migrating from the upgradient former Consolidated Metalworks facility at 4350 Industrial Corridor Drive, Rockford — immediately adjacent to GRS's facility at 4200 Industrial Corridor Drive.

Consolidated Metalworks operated a degreasing operation from 1968 to 1994 and is listed on the NPL. Vinyl chloride is a common degradation product of chlorinated solvents (PCE → TCE → DCE → vinyl chloride), which is exactly what you'd expect from a former degreasing operation. The groundwater flow direction at the site runs from the Consolidated Metalworks parcel toward GRS's SWMU-4. Dr. Sheffield's modeling suggests the vinyl chloride plume at MW-12 is more consistent with an off-site upgradient source than with anything in GRS's Landfill Cell B.

Here's what I need in the markup:

First — and this is **non-negotiable** — the decree must include an **express reservation of GRS's rights** to seek contribution from Consolidated Metalworks (or its successors, or the federal government if there's a CERCLA trust) under CERCLA § 113(f) and any applicable state-law contribution theories. Under current law, a consent decree that resolves CERCLA liability can trigger contribution protection, but it can also extinguish contribution claims if not carefully drafted. We absolutely cannot let this decree silently waive GRS's rights against third-party sources.

Second, I want you to propose language in the alternative:

- **Option A (our opening position):** Exclude SWMU-4 from the corrective action scope entirely, pending resolution of the source allocation through the ongoing NPL process.
- **Option B (where I expect we'll land):** Include SWMU-4 but with an express proviso that GRS's remediation obligation is limited to contamination attributable to GRS's operations, and that GRS reserves all rights to seek contribution, cost recovery, or offset for contamination attributable to off-site sources.

My preference is Option B — outright exclusion of SWMU-4 may be a bridge too far for Calloway. But I want to start with Option A and negotiate to Option B.

Please coordinate with Dr. Sheffield at Terravance to make sure the technical support for the off-site source theory is solid enough to reference in the markup comments. If Ian has any updated groundwater flow modeling or isotopic analysis, now is the time to get it.

---

**4. OTHER ISSUES TO ADDRESS IN THE MARKUP**

The following are shorter-form items I want you to cover. I'm not giving you the same level of detail here — you know how to draft these — but I'm flagging them so nothing falls through the cracks.

**(a) Privilege waiver (Section 14.2).** This one is obvious — they're demanding access to privileged communications. No. Carve it out. This should not be controversial; even Calloway will expect us to redline this. Limit disclosure to non-privileged environmental records, sampling data, monitoring reports, and the like. Cite the standard formulation.

**(b) Stipulated penalties — no cure period (Section 9.1).** The escalating penalties ($5K/$10K/$25K per day) with no notice-and-cure period and no cap are aggressive. Standard practice is a 15- to 30-day cure period after written notice before penalties begin accruing. Propose 30 days with written notice, and an aggregate cap — I'd start at $1.5 million total and expect to land around $2–3 million. Also make sure there's an exception for de minimis or technical violations.

**(c) Reopener clause (Section 18.1).** Overly broad. Needs a materiality threshold and a causal nexus requirement — the reopener should only apply to conditions caused by GRS operations, not off-site migration (this ties directly into the Consolidated Metalworks issue). Also should be limited to information not known or reasonably available at the time of settlement. Push for EPA model reopener language.

**(d) SEP administration by FRC.** I know Dr. Okafor's group wants to run the $2.0 million wetlands restoration, but having an adverse party administer the SEP is a conflict. Propose either an independent third-party administrator or a joint oversight committee with GRS audit rights. The amount is fine — don't fight the $2 million number.

**(e) FRC facility access (Section 14.1).** FRC getting the same unrestricted, unannounced access rights as Illinois EPA is unusual for a citizen-suit intervenor. Limit FRC to quarterly progress reports and annual site visits with 10 business days' notice, accompanied by GRS personnel. The State's access is fine — they're the regulator.

**(f) 30-year monitoring with no off-ramp (Section 12.4).** 30 years of quarterly monitoring regardless of results is excessive. Propose adaptive monitoring: step down to semi-annual after 5 years of compliance, annual after 10 years, and allow termination after 4 consecutive years meeting all standards with a minimum floor of 10 years total. Reference EPA's performance-based monitoring guidance.

**(g) No force majeure provision.** There's no force majeure clause at all. We need one. Standard language — events beyond GRS's reasonable control, including but not limited to natural disasters, supply chain disruptions, regulatory changes, and discovery of unexpected subsurface conditions. Notice requirement of 10 business days, with documentation. This is a conforming/technical addition that should not be controversial.

**(h) Natural attenuation at SWMU-3.** Make sure the decree doesn't foreclose monitored natural attenuation as a potential remedy at SWMU-3. Terravance's modeling shows MNA could reduce SWMU-3 costs from $4.1 million to approximately $1.2 million — a $2.9 million savings. The CMS should be required to evaluate MNA as a remedy alternative. Don't commit us to MNA in the decree, but make sure it's on the table for the CMS.

---

**5. WHAT NOT TO FIGHT ABOUT**

Equally important — here's what to leave alone:

- **The $3.75 million civil penalty amount.** Tom doesn't love it but we can live with it. The exposure at trial is worse.
- **The 12-month CMS timeline.** With the RI substantially complete, this is doable. Don't flag it.
- **The $600,000 FRC payment** ($475K fees + $125K consultant costs). This is within the range of reasonable. Contesting it would antagonize Margaret Andrade and, more importantly, Judge Sung.
- **Quarterly monitoring frequency during active remediation.** Standard. The problem is the 30-year duration and no adaptive provisions, not the frequency itself.
- **The $2.0 million SEP amount.** The issue is who administers it, not how much.

---

**6. PROCESS AND LOGISTICS**

Deliverables I need by September 30:

1. **Redlined consent decree** — tracked changes with margin comments explaining the basis for each revision.
2. **Cover memo** summarizing all changes, the rationale for each, risk assessment (i.e., which items we expect pushback on and which should be noncontroversial), and items needing further client input or technical support.

Please make sure you've reviewed carefully:

- The proposed Consent Decree (proposed-consent-decree.docx) — the September 8 version from Calloway's office
- The Terravance RI Summary Memorandum (terravance-ri-summary.docx) — the January 15, 2023 draft
- The GRS financial summary (grs-financial-summary.xlsx) — the Excel workbook from Sandra's finance team with P&L, balance sheet, and credit facility details
- The FRC demand letter (frc-demand-letter.docx) — from Margaret S. Andrade at Kessler, Andrade & Yun

Call Dr. Sheffield at Terravance if you need any technical clarification on the MNA modeling or the off-site source analysis at SWMU-4. Don't be shy about that — Ian knows this project cold and he's responsive.

I'll be in depositions in another matter September 23–26 but available by email. I'll block time to review your draft on October 1.

Reminder: mark everything PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT. The markup itself will eventually be shared with Calloway's office, but the cover memo and this email are internal only.

---

This is a good settlement if we can fix the structural problems. Tom and Sandra are pragmatic — they want a deal, not a war. But the financial assurance and covenant issues are dealbreakers if we can't move Calloway off his current positions.

Let me know if you have questions. Happy to jump on a call tomorrow morning.

Rachel

---

**Rachel A. Downing**
Partner
Hartwell, Brannigan & Locke LLP
150 N. Wacker Drive, Suite 3200
Chicago, IL 60606
rdowning@hbl-law.com

---

This communication contains attorney work product and is protected by the attorney-client privilege. 5	
6	**TECHNICAL MEMORANDUM**
7	
8	**TO:** Sandra K. Frey, General Counsel, Greenfield Recycling Solutions, Inc. Rachel A. Downing, Esq., Hartwell, Brannigan & Locke LLP
9	
10	**CC:** Kevin M. Pratt, Esq., Hartwell, Brannigan & Locke LLP Thomas R. Ellison, Chief Executive Officer, Greenfield Recycling Solutions, Inc.
11	
12	**FROM:** Dr. Ian W. Sheffield, P.E., Lead Consultant, Terravance Environmental Group, LLC
13	
14	**DATE:** January 15, 2023
15	
16	**RE:** Summary of Remedial Investigation Findings --- GRS Rockford Facility, 4200 Industrial Corridor Drive, Rockford, Illinois 61101; RCRA Permit No. ILD-098-721-445; Case No. 2021-CH-00847 (Circuit Court of Winnebago County, Illinois, Seventeenth Judicial Circuit)
17	
18	**[1. Purpose and Scope]{.underline}**
19	
20	This memorandum summarizes the findings of the Remedial Investigation (\"RI\") conducted by Terravance Environmental Group, LLC (\"Terravance\") at the Greenfield Recycling Solutions, Inc. (\"GRS\") Rockford Facility located at 4200 Industrial Corridor Drive, Rockford, Illinois 61101 (the \"Facility\" or \"Site\"). The purpose of this summary is to present the key findings of the RI in a format accessible to counsel and GRS management, to identify areas of agreement and disagreement with the State\'s environmental consultant, and to provide technical recommendations relevant to the ongoing litigation and anticipated settlement discussions.
21	
22	The RI was conducted pursuant to the corrective action obligations imposed under GRS\'s Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (\"RCRA\") Part B Permit No. ILD-098-721-445 and in connection with the enforcement action currently pending as Case No. 2021-CH-00847 in the Circuit Court of Winnebago County, Illinois, Seventeenth Judicial Circuit, the Honorable Patricia Sung presiding. The parties to that action include the State of Illinois, acting through the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency (\"Illinois EPA\") and the Office of the Illinois Attorney General, Environmental Bureau (Deputy Bureau Chief Martin J. Calloway), as plaintiff, and the Fox River Conservancy (\"FRC\"), a not-for-profit environmental organization (Executive Director Dr. Lena M. Okafor), as citizen-suit intervenor-plaintiff, having been granted intervenor status on October 14, 2021.
23	
24	The draft RI report was submitted to Illinois EPA on January 15, 2023, concurrent with the issuance of this summary memorandum. This memorandum references but does not reproduce the full technical data, boring logs, well construction details, laboratory analytical reports, and modeling results contained in the draft RI report.
25	
26	The scope of the RI encompassed the investigation of five designated areas at the Facility: Solid Waste Management Unit 1 (\"SWMU-1\"), Solid Waste Management Unit 2 (\"SWMU-2\"), Solid Waste Management Unit 3 (\"SWMU-3\"), Solid Waste Management Unit 4 (\"SWMU-4\"), and Area of Concern 1 (\"AOC-1\"). The investigation included soil, sediment, and groundwater characterization across all five areas. The State\'s environmental consultant is Clarendon Technical Services, Inc. (\"Clarendon\"), located at 225 West Washington Street, Suite 1400, Springfield, Illinois 62701. As detailed in this memorandum, Terravance has certain significant disagreements with Clarendon\'s interpretations and recommendations, particularly with respect to SWMU-3 and SWMU-4.
27	
28	The RI was conducted in accordance with the applicable regulatory standards, including the Illinois Environmental Protection Act, 415 ILCS 5/ et seq., the Illinois Administrative Code provisions governing the Tiered Approach to Corrective Action Objectives at 35 IAC Part 742, the Groundwater Quality Standards at 35 IAC Part 620, and the applicable conditions of GRS\'s RCRA Subtitle C permit.
29	
30	GRS is a Delaware corporation (EIN: 36-4821097) that has operated at the Rockford Facility since 2009. The Facility processes municipal solid waste, construction and demolition (\"C&D\") debris, and electronic waste. GRS employs approximately 420 individuals across all of its facilities. The enforcement proceedings arose from a March 2020 Illinois EPA compliance inspection that identified permit violations at the Facility, which was followed by a Violation Notice issued June 15, 2020, a Complaint and Compliance Order issued September 2, 2020, a referral to the Illinois Attorney General\'s Office on February 10, 2021, the filing of the State\'s complaint on April 22, 2021, the filing of FRC\'s citizen-suit complaint on July 8, 2021, and the Court\'s order granting FRC intervenor-plaintiff status on October 14, 2021.
31	
32	**[2. Investigation Methodology]{.underline}**
33	
34	Terravance conducted the RI field activities between March 2022 and November 2022 in accordance with the RI Work Plan approved by Illinois EPA on January 28, 2022. The following is a summary of the principal field investigation activities and analytical methods employed during the RI.
35	
36	**Soil Boring Program.** Terravance advanced a total of forty-seven (47) soil borings across the five investigation areas. Borings were advanced using hollow-stem auger and direct-push (Geoprobe) methods to depths ranging from ten (10) to forty (40) feet below ground surface (\"bgs\"), depending on the area of investigation and the lithologic conditions encountered. The boring program included sixteen (16) borings at SWMU-1, eight (8) borings at SWMU-2, ten (10) borings at SWMU-3, eight (8) borings at SWMU-4, and five (5) borings at AOC-1. Soil samples were collected at two-foot intervals in the zone of suspected contamination and at five-foot intervals below that zone. Split-spoon samples were collected for laboratory analysis and lithologic characterization.
37	
38	**Groundwater Monitoring Well Installation and Sampling.** In addition to sampling the existing monitoring well network (wells MW-1 through MW-10, installed between 2010 and 2020), Terravance installed five (5) new monitoring wells (MW-11 through MW-15) to fill data gaps identified during the RI planning process. Key monitoring wells referenced in this memorandum include MW-7 and MW-9 (downgradient and lateral wells associated with the SWMU-3 dissolved-phase plume), MW-11 (installed between the Consolidated Metalworks property and SWMU-4 to evaluate potential upgradient source contributions), and MW-12 (downgradient of Landfill Cell B at SWMU-4). Groundwater samples were collected during four quarterly sampling events (March 2022, June 2022, September 2022, and December 2022) using low-flow purging and sampling techniques consistent with EPA Region 5 guidance.
39	
40	**Sediment Sampling.** Sediment samples were collected from SWMU-2 (Process Water Lagoon) and AOC-1 (Stormwater Outfall to the unnamed tributary). A total of twenty-two (22) sediment samples were collected using hand auger and Ponar grab sampling methods.
41	
42	**Laboratory Analytical Methods.** All samples were analyzed by Midwest Analytical Laboratories, Inc., an Illinois EPA-accredited laboratory, using EPA SW-846 methods, including Method 8260 for volatile organic compounds (\"VOCs\"), Method 8270 for semi-volatile organic compounds (\"SVOCs\"), Method 6010 (ICP-OES) for metals, and Method 7470 for mercury. Chain-of-custody procedures were maintained throughout sample collection, transport, and analysis. Quality assurance and quality control (\"QA/QC\") procedures included the collection and analysis of field duplicates, equipment rinsate blanks, and trip blanks, all in accordance with the approved Quality Assurance Project Plan (\"QAPP\").
43	
44	**Hydrogeological Assessment.** Terravance conducted a comprehensive hydrogeological evaluation of Site conditions, including measurement of groundwater elevations across the monitoring well network during each quarterly event, calculation of horizontal hydraulic gradients, and slug testing to determine hydraulic conductivity values for the shallow sand and gravel aquifer underlying the Site. The hydrogeological assessment confirmed that groundwater flow is generally from the northeast to the southwest across the Facility, with a horizontal gradient of approximately 0.008 feet per foot. This flow direction is critical to the off-site source analysis at SWMU-4, as discussed in Section 3.4 below.
45	
46	**Waste Identification.** The RI identified the following listed and characteristic hazardous wastes historically managed at the Facility: F001 through F005 (spent solvents from cleaning and degreasing operations), D006 (cadmium-bearing waste), D007 (chromium-bearing waste), and D008 (lead-bearing waste).
47	
48	**Fate and Transport Modeling.** Terravance conducted fate and transport modeling for the dissolved-phase chlorinated VOC plumes at SWMU-3 and SWMU-4, utilizing the BIOSCREEN analytical model to evaluate natural attenuation processes and to project the future migration and attenuation of the dissolved-phase plumes under current conditions. The modeling approach, input parameters, and results are discussed in Sections 3.3 and 3.4 below and are presented in full in the draft RI report at Appendix G.
49	
50	**[3. Site Conditions and Findings by Investigation Area]{.underline}**
51	
52	**[3.1 SWMU-1 --- Former Drum Storage Area]{.underline}**
53	
54	SWMU-1 consists of a former outdoor drum storage area located in the northwestern portion of the Facility, encompassing an area of approximately 0.75 acres. The area was historically used for the temporary storage of drums containing spent solvents, battery residues, and other waste materials generated during GRS\'s electronic waste processing operations. Drum storage operations at this location ceased in 2017 when GRS constructed a new enclosed drum storage building on the eastern side of the Facility. The former drum storage area is now an unpaved, graded surface underlain by fill material consisting of sand, gravel, and cinders to a depth of approximately six to eight feet, overlying native glacial till.
55	
56	The primary contaminant of concern at SWMU-1 is lead (RCRA characteristic D008). Soil sampling across the sixteen borings advanced at SWMU-1 revealed lead concentrations ranging from 85 mg/kg to a maximum of 2,100 mg/kg. The maximum detected concentration of 2,100 mg/kg exceeds the Tier 1 residential remediation objective (\"RO\") of 400 mg/kg established under 35 IAC Part 742 by a factor of approximately 5.25. Lead contamination is concentrated in the upper four to six feet of fill material, with concentrations decreasing sharply below the fill horizon. No significant lead contamination was detected in the native glacial till below the fill. The lateral extent of lead contamination above the Tier 1 residential RO defines an approximately 0.75-acre footprint, consistent with the historical drum storage area boundaries.
57	
58	Groundwater monitoring data from wells MW-1 and MW-2, located downgradient of SWMU-1, did not reveal significant dissolved-phase lead above Class I groundwater quality standards. The limited mobility of lead in the Site soils is consistent with the neutral to slightly alkaline pH (7.1 to 7.6) and the significant clay content of the native glacial till underlying the fill material, which acts as a natural barrier to downward migration.
59	
60	The estimated cost to remediate SWMU-1 is approximately \$1,800,000, based on excavation and off-site disposal of impacted soils (estimated volume of approximately 4,800 cubic yards) at a permitted disposal facility, followed by backfill with imported clean material, re-grading, and site restoration. This is a straightforward excavation-based remedy. Terravance concurs with Clarendon\'s characterization of contamination extent and the presumptive remedial approach for SWMU-1.
61	
62	**[3.2 SWMU-2 --- Process Water Lagoon]{.underline}**
63	
64	SWMU-2 consists of an unlined surface impoundment (the \"Process Water Lagoon\") located in the central-western portion of the Facility. The lagoon historically received process wastewater generated by GRS\'s electronic waste processing operations, including rinse water from circuit board processing, leachate from electronic waste storage, and equipment wash water. The lagoon measures approximately 150 feet in length by 80 feet in width, with an average depth of approximately six feet. The lagoon was constructed in 2010 and has operated continuously as a wastewater receiving impoundment, though GRS initiated a partial wastewater diversion program in 2019 that reduced influent volumes.
65	
66	The primary contaminant of concern at SWMU-2 is cadmium (RCRA characteristic D006). Sediment sampling within the lagoon revealed cadmium concentrations ranging from 18 mg/kg to a maximum of 78 mg/kg. The maximum detected concentration of 78 mg/kg exceeds the applicable remediation objective of 37 mg/kg under 35 IAC Part 742 by a factor of approximately 2.11. Additionally, chromium (RCRA characteristic D007) was detected in lagoon sediments at concentrations up to 185 mg/kg, which is elevated relative to regional background levels and warrants further evaluation during the Corrective Measures Study (\"CMS\").
67	
68	Groundwater monitoring data from wells MW-3 and MW-4, located downgradient of SWMU-2, show dissolved cadmium concentrations at levels exceeding the Class I groundwater quality standard under 35 IAC Part 620, confirming that the unlined lagoon has contributed to groundwater contamination beneath the impoundment. Cadmium concentrations in downgradient groundwater, while above the applicable standard, are not indicative of a large-scale dissolved-phase plume, and the impact appears to be localized to the immediate vicinity of the lagoon.
69	
70	The estimated cost to remediate SWMU-2 is approximately \$2,400,000. The anticipated remedial approach includes lagoon dewatering and treatment of impounded water, excavation and off-site disposal of impacted sediments (estimated volume of approximately 2,700 cubic yards), installation of a synthetic liner or, alternatively, permanent closure of the lagoon in accordance with RCRA closure requirements, and implementation of a groundwater monitoring program to verify attenuation of cadmium in downgradient wells. Terravance concurs with Clarendon\'s characterization of the nature and extent of contamination at SWMU-2 and with the general remedial approach.
71	
72	**[3.3 SWMU-3 --- Loading Dock / Drainage Swale]{.underline}**
73	
74	SWMU-3 encompasses the paved loading dock area and an adjacent unpaved drainage swale located on the eastern side of the Facility. The loading dock was used for the receipt and transfer of containerized waste, including drums of spent chlorinated solvents (F001 through F005 listed wastes). Historical records and facility personnel interviews confirm that spills of chlorinated solvents occurred in this area during waste handling operations, particularly during the period from 2011 to 2016 before GRS implemented enhanced spill containment measures. The drainage swale adjacent to the loading dock conveyed surface water runoff from the loading area to the facility\'s stormwater management system.
75	
76	The primary contaminants of concern at SWMU-3 are tetrachloroethylene (\"PCE\") in subsurface soils and trichloroethylene (\"TCE\") in groundwater. Soil sampling at SWMU-3 revealed PCE at concentrations up to 14.2 mg/kg in subsurface soils at a depth of approximately eight to ten feet below ground surface. This concentration exceeds the Tier 1 residential remediation objective of 0.46 mg/kg under 35 IAC Part 742 by a factor of approximately 30.9. TCE was detected in groundwater at monitoring well MW-7, located approximately 200 feet downgradient of the loading dock source area, at a concentration of 28.4 µg/L, which exceeds the Class I groundwater quality standard of 5 µg/L under 35 IAC 620.410 by a factor of approximately 5.68. TCE was also detected at monitoring well MW-9, located lateral to the plume centerline approximately 250 feet downgradient, at a concentration of 19.7 µg/L, which exceeds the Class I standard by a factor of approximately 3.94.
77	
78	The dissolved-phase TCE plume extends approximately 600 feet downgradient (southwest) from the SWMU-3 source area, as defined by isoconcentration mapping based on the monitoring well network data. PCE, present in subsurface soils at the source area, is the parent compound undergoing sequential reductive dechlorination in the subsurface to produce TCE, cis-1,2-dichloroethylene (\"cis-1,2-DCE\"), and vinyl chloride as daughter products. The detection of these daughter products in the monitoring well data, combined with favorable geochemical indicators, provides clear evidence of active biodegradation processes in the subsurface at SWMU-3.
79	
80	**Monitored Natural Attenuation Evaluation.** Terravance conducted fate and transport modeling using the BIOSCREEN analytical solute transport model to evaluate monitored natural attenuation (\"MNA\") as a potential remedial alternative at SWMU-3. The modeling was conducted in accordance with the methodology described in EPA\'s OSWER Directive 9200.4-17P, *Use of Monitored Natural Attenuation at Superfund, RCRA Corrective Action, and Underground Storage Tank Sites* (April 1999), and incorporated site-specific parameters derived from the RI field data.
81	
82	The key modeling parameters included: first-order biodecay rates for TCE derived from the observed concentration trends at MW-7 and MW-9 over the 2020--2022 monitoring period (half-life of approximately 2.8 years); retardation factors calculated from site-specific organic carbon content of the aquifer solids; groundwater seepage velocity of approximately 75 feet per year based on measured hydraulic conductivity (3.2 × 10⁻³ cm/sec), hydraulic gradient (0.008 ft/ft), and effective porosity (0.25); and current plume dimensions as defined by the RI characterization data.
83	
84	The key finding of Terravance\'s modeling is that natural attenuation processes, without active remediation, are projected to reduce TCE concentrations below the 5 µg/L Class I groundwater quality standard at all monitoring points within the SWMU-3 plume within a timeframe of approximately eight to ten years. This conclusion is supported by three independent lines of evidence:
85	
86	First, declining concentration trends have been observed over the 2020--2022 monitoring period at both MW-7 and MW-9. TCE at MW-7 has declined from 42.1 µg/L (March 2020) to 28.4 µg/L (December 2022), representing a reduction of approximately 33% over the monitoring period. TCE at MW-9 has declined from 31.8 µg/L (March 2020) to 19.7 µg/L (December 2022), a reduction of approximately 38%. These declining trends are statistically significant and consistent with active attenuation processes.
87	
88	Second, geochemical indicators at SWMU-3 are favorable for reductive dechlorination. Dissolved oxygen concentrations in the plume core are consistently below 1.0 mg/L, indicating anaerobic conditions conducive to biological reductive dechlorination. Ferrous iron concentrations are elevated (4.2 to 8.7 mg/L), indicating iron-reducing conditions. The presence of cis-1,2-DCE and trace vinyl chloride as daughter products confirms that the sequential dechlorination pathway is active.
89	
90	Third, isoconcentration mapping demonstrates a stable to shrinking plume footprint over the monitoring period. The 5 µg/L TCE isoconcentration contour has not expanded between the March 2020 and December 2022 sampling events, and the area enclosed by the 10 µg/L contour has decreased by approximately 15%.
91	
92	EPA\'s OSWER Directive 9200.4-17P establishes that MNA is an appropriate remedial technology, recognized by EPA for application at RCRA corrective action sites, where these three lines of evidence --- concentration trends, geochemical indicators, and modeling --- support its effectiveness. The NCP remedy selection framework at 40 CFR 300.430(e) requires evaluation of remedial alternatives against nine criteria, including long-term effectiveness and permanence, reduction of toxicity/mobility/volume through treatment, short-term effectiveness, implementability, and cost. MNA should be evaluated against these criteria as a remedy alternative in the forthcoming CMS.
93	
94	**Clarendon\'s Position.** Clarendon Technical Services insists on active pump-and-treat with air stripping as the presumptive remedy for the SWMU-3 dissolved-phase TCE plume. To Terravance\'s knowledge, Clarendon has not conducted independent fate and transport modeling and has not rebutted Terravance\'s attenuation data or modeling results. Clarendon\'s position appears to be based primarily on the magnitude of current exceedances --- TCE at 28.4 µg/L at MW-7 is approximately 5.7 times the Class I standard --- rather than on an evaluation of concentration trends, geochemical conditions, or plume stability. Terravance respectfully submits that the current magnitude of exceedances, while relevant, does not in itself justify foreclosing evaluation of MNA as a remedy alternative when the data demonstrate active attenuation and a declining plume.
95	
96	**Cost Comparison.** The estimated cost of active remediation at SWMU-3 via pump-and-treat with air stripping, as currently scoped by Clarendon, is approximately \$4,100,000, including system design and construction, operation and maintenance over an estimated fifteen-year operational period, effluent treatment and discharge, and system decommissioning. The estimated cost of MNA with long-term monitoring at SWMU-3 is approximately \$1,200,000, including quarterly groundwater monitoring for a projected period of ten years, periodic model validation, and reporting. The potential cost savings of selecting MNA over pump-and-treat at SWMU-3 is therefore approximately \$2,900,000.
97	
98	**Terravance Recommendation.** Terravance strongly recommends that MNA be preserved as a viable remedial alternative in the forthcoming CMS. The data collected during the RI provides robust lines of evidence supporting MNA at SWMU-3. Foreclosing MNA at this stage of the proceedings --- whether in the settlement framework or in the Consent Decree --- would be inconsistent with EPA guidance, the NCP framework, and sound remedial practice. Terravance recommends that any settlement framework explicitly allow MNA to be evaluated during the CMS process and that the CMS be structured to conduct a rigorous, side-by-side comparison of active remediation and MNA consistent with EPA\'s OSWER Directive 9200.4-17P and the NCP nine-criteria analysis.
99	
100	If MNA is ultimately selected as the remedy for SWMU-3, the total estimated remediation cost for all five investigation areas would be reduced from \$10,800,000 to approximately \$7,900,000, with corresponding reductions in the financial assurance obligations that will be required under the Consent Decree.
101	
102	**[3.4 SWMU-4 --- Landfill Cell B]{.underline}**
103	
104	SWMU-4 encompasses Landfill Cell B, a closed landfill cell located in the northeastern portion of the Facility. Landfill Cell B received construction and demolition debris and certain industrial wastes from approximately 2011 through 2018, when the cell was closed and capped with a low-permeability soil cover in accordance with permit conditions. The waste profile for Landfill Cell B, based on GRS\'s waste manifests and operating records, consists predominantly of C&D debris (concrete, brick, asphalt, wood, drywall), with limited quantities of non-hazardous industrial waste from GRS\'s recycling operations. Notably, the waste records for Landfill Cell B do not include chlorinated solvents, spent solvent wastes (F001--F005), or waste streams containing PCE or TCE.
105	
106	The contaminant of concern at SWMU-4 is vinyl chloride in groundwater. Monitoring well MW-12, located approximately 100 feet downgradient (southwest) of Landfill Cell B, shows vinyl chloride at a concentration of 3.8 µg/L, which exceeds the Class I groundwater quality standard of 2.0 µg/L under 35 IAC 620.410 by a factor of approximately 1.90. The estimated cost of remediation at SWMU-4, as currently scoped, is approximately \$1,900,000, which includes installation of a groundwater extraction and treatment system and long-term monitoring.
107	
108	**Off-Site Source Analysis.** Terravance\'s investigation identified strong evidence that the vinyl chloride contamination detected at MW-12 may originate, in whole or in part, from an upgradient, off-site source --- specifically, the former Consolidated Metalworks facility located at 4350 Industrial Corridor Drive, Rockford, Illinois 61101.
109	
110	Consolidated Metalworks operated a metal degreasing operation at 4350 Industrial Corridor Drive from approximately 1968 to 1994. The degreasing operation utilized large volumes of chlorinated solvents, primarily TCE and PCE, as degreasing agents. The Consolidated Metalworks facility is listed on the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (\"CERCLA\") National Priorities List (\"NPL\") and has been the subject of federal Superfund investigation and remediation activities since the mid-1990s. TCE and PCE are well-established precursors to vinyl chloride through the process of sequential reductive dechlorination in groundwater systems.
111	
112	The hydrogeological evidence supports an off-site source contribution. As confirmed by the RI hydrogeological assessment, groundwater flow in the vicinity of SWMU-4 is from the northeast to the southwest. The Consolidated Metalworks facility is located northeast of GRS\'s Landfill Cell B --- that is, directly upgradient. The nearest point of the Consolidated Metalworks property boundary is approximately 150 feet northeast of the GRS property boundary. Groundwater migrating from the Consolidated Metalworks site would flow toward and beneath SWMU-4 before reaching MW-12.
113	
114	Geochemical evidence further supports the off-site source theory through multiple converging lines of evidence:
115	
116	\(a\) The vinyl chloride concentrations detected at MW-12 (3.8 µg/L) are inconsistent with the waste types deposited in Landfill Cell B. The cell received primarily C&D debris and non-hazardous industrial waste, not chlorinated solvents. There is no mechanism by which C&D debris would generate vinyl chloride in groundwater.
117	
118	\(b\) Monitoring well MW-11, installed by Terravance during the RI at a location between the Consolidated Metalworks property and MW-12 (approximately 75 feet northeast of the GRS property boundary), shows detectable TCE at 7.2 µg/L and cis-1,2-DCE at 12.5 µg/L. The presence of these chlorinated ethene compounds in a well located upgradient of both Landfill Cell B and MW-12, and between the GRS property and the Consolidated Metalworks site, is strongly indicative of a dissolved-phase plume migrating from the direction of the Consolidated Metalworks facility. TCE and cis-1,2-DCE are intermediate degradation products in the reductive dechlorination sequence from PCE to vinyl chloride; their presence at MW-11 demonstrates that the dechlorination sequence is active in the upgradient groundwater, producing vinyl chloride as an end product at MW-12.
119	
120	\(c\) Compound-specific isotope analysis (\"CSIA\") was performed on vinyl chloride samples collected from MW-12. The carbon isotope ratios (δ¹³C) of vinyl chloride at MW-12 are enriched relative to values typical of biogenic vinyl chloride production from landfill-derived organic matter. The δ¹³C signature is more consistent with the degradation of industrial-grade TCE of the type historically used in vapor degreasing operations, such as those conducted at the Consolidated Metalworks facility. The full CSIA results and interpretation are presented in the draft RI report at Appendix H.
121	
122	\(d\) GRS has not historically used or stored TCE or PCE at or near Landfill Cell B. GRS\'s chlorinated solvent handling was confined to the SWMU-3 area (Loading Dock), which is located on the eastern side of the Facility, approximately 800 feet from SWMU-4. The SWMU-3 and SWMU-4 areas are hydrogeologically disconnected --- they are located in different portions of the Facility and are not connected by a groundwater flow path. The SWMU-3 TCE plume migrates to the southwest from the loading dock area and does not approach SWMU-4.
123	
124	**Terravance Conclusion on SWMU-4.** Based on the hydrogeological evidence, the geochemical data, the MW-11 upgradient detections, the CSIA results, and the absence of any chlorinated solvent source within Landfill Cell B, Terravance concludes that the vinyl chloride detected at MW-12 is more likely attributable to upgradient migration from the NPL-listed Consolidated Metalworks facility than to GRS\'s operations at Landfill Cell B. Assigning sole remediation responsibility for SWMU-4 groundwater contamination to GRS is not supported by the technical evidence developed during the RI.
125	
126	**Recommendations Regarding SWMU-4.** Terravance recommends the following course of action with respect to SWMU-4:
127	
128	\(1\) SWMU-4 should be excluded from the scope of GRS\'s corrective action obligations under the Consent Decree, or, alternatively, GRS\'s remediation obligations at SWMU-4 should be limited to those conditions demonstrated to originate from GRS operations at Landfill Cell B, to the extent any such conditions exist.
129	
130	\(2\) GRS should preserve its contribution rights under CERCLA Section 113(f) and applicable state law against Consolidated Metalworks and any other potentially responsible parties (\"PRPs\") associated with the Consolidated Metalworks NPL site for costs incurred in addressing contamination attributable to the Consolidated Metalworks facility.
131	
132	\(3\) Additional investigation should be conducted to further define the relative contributions of GRS and Consolidated Metalworks to the vinyl chloride contamination at MW-12. This investigation should include the installation of at least two additional monitoring wells along the northeastern property boundary and expanded CSIA sampling at MW-11, MW-12, and the new monitoring points.
133	
134	\(4\) Any settlement framework should account for the off-site source evidence and should not foreclose GRS\'s ability to seek cost recovery or contribution from responsible parties for the Consolidated Metalworks contamination. The Consent Decree should include a reservation of rights or contribution protection provisions that preserve GRS\'s ability to pursue these claims.
135	
136	If SWMU-4 is excluded from GRS\'s remediation scope, the total estimated remediation cost would decrease from \$10,800,000 to approximately \$8,900,000.
137	
138	**[3.5 AOC-1 --- Stormwater Outfall to Tributary]{.underline}**
139	
140	AOC-1 consists of the stormwater discharge point where facility surface water runoff enters an unnamed tributary of the Rock River watershed. This discharge point is located at the southwestern boundary of the Facility, where the facility\'s stormwater management system conveys collected runoff through a 24-inch corrugated metal pipe outfall into the unnamed tributary. The unnamed tributary flows generally westward for approximately 1.2 miles before entering Kilbuck Creek, which is a direct tributary of the Rock River. The FRC cited this discharge pathway in its citizen-suit complaint, alleging that facility-derived contaminants are entering the Rock River watershed through this stormwater outfall and adversely affecting water quality in streams feeding into the Rock River.
141	
142	The primary contaminant of concern at AOC-1 is chromium (RCRA characteristic D007) in sediment. Sediment sampling downstream of the stormwater outfall revealed chromium concentrations up to 210 mg/kg. While there is no site-specific remediation objective for chromium in sediment applicable under the current permit conditions, the detected concentration is significantly elevated relative to regional background sediment concentrations, which were measured at five upstream reference locations at concentrations ranging from 22 to 38 mg/kg. The lateral extent of chromium impact in sediment extends approximately 200 linear feet downstream of the outfall, with concentrations decreasing to background levels beyond that distance.
143	
144	The estimated cost to remediate AOC-1 is approximately \$600,000, encompassing removal and off-site disposal of impacted sediments from the 200-foot affected reach (estimated volume of approximately 320 cubic yards), repair and improvement of the stormwater outfall structure, installation of erosion and sediment controls, and post-remediation monitoring. Terravance concurs with Clarendon\'s characterization of the nature and extent of contamination at AOC-1 and with the general approach to remediation.

**[7. Technical Disputes with Clarendon Technical Services]{.underline}**

**[7.1 SWMU-3 --- Active Remediation vs. Monitored Natural Attenuation]{.underline}**

As described in Section 3.3, Clarendon Technical Services has taken the position that active pump-and-treat with air stripping is the sole appropriate remedy for the dissolved-phase TCE plume at SWMU-3, at an estimated cost of \$4,100,000. Terravance disagrees with this position for the following reasons.

First, Clarendon has not provided any independent fate and transport modeling to support its position that active remediation is necessary. Terravance\'s modeling, using site-specific parameters derived from the RI data and the BIOSCREEN analytical model, projects that natural attenuation will reduce TCE concentrations below the 5 µg/L Class I standard within eight to ten years. Clarendon has not attempted to rebut this modeling, nor has it offered alternative modeling results or identified specific deficiencies in Terravance\'s modeling methodology or input parameters.

Second, Clarendon\'s recommendation appears to be based primarily on the magnitude of current exceedances --- TCE at MW-7 is approximately 5.7 times the Class I standard --- without giving adequate weight to the demonstrated declining concentration trends, the favorable geochemical conditions, or the stable-to-shrinking plume footprint. The current magnitude of an exceedance is only one factor in remedy selection; trend analysis and evaluation of natural attenuation processes are equally important considerations under established EPA guidance.

Third, EPA\'s OSWER Directive 9200.4-17P explicitly establishes that MNA is appropriate at RCRA corrective action sites where three lines of evidence are present: (1) historical trend data showing declining concentrations; (2) hydrogeochemical data demonstrating active degradation processes; and (3) modeling confirming plume stability and projected timeframe to achieve cleanup standards. All three lines of evidence are present at SWMU-3, as documented in Section 3.3 of this memorandum and in Appendix G of the draft RI report.

Fourth, the CMS --- which the proposed Consent Decree will require to be completed within twelve months of entry --- is the appropriate vehicle for evaluating and comparing remedy alternatives, including both active remediation and MNA. Precluding MNA from the settlement framework or mandating active remediation at SWMU-3 in advance of the CMS evaluation would be inconsistent with the NCP remedy selection process at 40 CFR 300.430(e) and would deprive GRS of the opportunity to present a technically and economically viable remedy alternative to the Court and Illinois EPA.

Terravance strongly recommends that the settlement terms not foreclose MNA as a remedy to be evaluated during the CMS. Preserving MNA as a remedy alternative could result in cost savings of approximately \$2,900,000 at SWMU-3 alone, with corresponding reductions in GRS\'s financial assurance obligations.

**[7.2 SWMU-4 --- Source Attribution]{.underline}**

As described in Section 3.4, Clarendon attributes all vinyl chloride contamination at MW-12 to GRS operations at Landfill Cell B. Terravance disagrees with this attribution for the following reasons.

First, Clarendon has not conducted any upgradient source evaluation at or near SWMU-4. Clarendon did not install monitoring wells between the Consolidated Metalworks property and SWMU-4, did not sample for chlorinated VOCs in the upgradient groundwater flow path, and did not evaluate historical operations at the Consolidated Metalworks facility as a potential source of the vinyl chloride detected at MW-12. By contrast, Terravance installed MW-11 specifically to evaluate this upgradient pathway and obtained data demonstrating detectable TCE and cis-1,2-DCE in groundwater migrating from the direction of the Consolidated Metalworks facility.

Second, Clarendon has not analyzed or addressed the CSIA data collected by Terravance, which provides isotopic evidence that the vinyl chloride at MW-12 is more consistent with degradation of industrial-grade TCE used in degreasing operations than with the waste profiles at Landfill Cell B.

Third, Clarendon has not accounted for the hydrogeological setting --- specifically, the fact that Consolidated Metalworks is located directly upgradient of SWMU-4 and MW-12, and that the documented groundwater flow direction (northeast to southwest) would carry any dissolved-phase plume from the Consolidated Metalworks site toward and through the SWMU-4 area.

Fourth, the vinyl chloride exceedance at MW-12 is relatively modest (3.8 µg/L vs. the 2.0 µg/L standard, an exceedance factor of only 1.9×), which is more consistent with the leading edge of a diffuse, off-site plume than with a point-source release from Landfill Cell B. If Landfill Cell B were the source, one would expect higher concentrations in the immediate vicinity of the cell and the presence of precursor compounds (TCE, PCE) in wells closer to the cell, neither of which has been observed.

Holding GRS solely responsible for SWMU-4 remediation in the absence of a proper source allocation study is technically unsupported and may expose GRS to remediation costs of approximately \$1,900,000 for contamination that it did not cause. Terravance recommends that the settlement framework account for the off-site source evidence and preserve GRS\'s ability to seek cost recovery or contribution from responsible parties associated with the Consolidated Metalworks NPL site.

**[8. Conclusions and Recommendations]{.underline}**

Based on the findings of the Remedial Investigation, Terravance offers the following conclusions and recommendations for consideration by GRS and its counsel:

**1. SWMU-1, SWMU-2, and AOC-1.** Contamination at SWMU-1 (Former Drum Storage Area), SWMU-2 (Process Water Lagoon), and AOC-1 (Stormwater Outfall to Tributary) is well-characterized and clearly attributable to GRS operations at the Facility. The nature and extent of contamination at these three areas is well-defined, and the presumptive remedial approaches are straightforward. The combined estimated remediation cost for these three areas is \$4,800,000 (\$1,800,000 + \$2,400,000 + \$600,000 = \$4,800,000). Terravance concurs with Clarendon\'s characterization of these three areas and considers the remediation cost estimates to be reasonable, subject to refinement during the CMS.

**2. SWMU-3 --- Monitored Natural Attenuation.** Contamination at SWMU-3 (Loading Dock / Drainage Swale) is attributable to GRS operations, but the appropriate remedy is subject to legitimate technical dispute. Terravance\'s fate and transport modeling and geochemical data provide three independent lines of evidence supporting MNA as a viable and potentially more cost-effective remedial alternative. The estimated cost of MNA (\$1,200,000) compares favorably to the estimated cost of active pump-and-treat (\$4,100,000), representing a potential savings of approximately \$2,900,000. Terravance recommends that:

> \(a\) MNA be explicitly preserved as a remedial alternative to be evaluated in the CMS;
>
> \(b\) The CMS be structured to evaluate MNA consistent with EPA\'s OSWER Directive 9200.4-17P and the NCP nine-criteria analysis at 40 CFR 300.430(e);
>
> \(c\) The settlement framework not mandate active remediation at SWMU-3 in advance of the CMS evaluation, as such a mandate would prejudge the remedy selection process and foreclose a technically sound and economically advantageous alternative; and
>
> \(d\) If MNA is ultimately selected as the remedy for SWMU-3, the total estimated remediation cost would decrease from \$10,800,000 to approximately \$7,900,000, with potential corresponding reductions in the financial assurance requirements under the Consent Decree.

**3. SWMU-4 --- Off-Site Source.** The technical evidence developed during the RI indicates that the vinyl chloride contamination detected at MW-12 may originate, in whole or in part, from the upgradient, NPL-listed Consolidated Metalworks facility rather than from GRS\'s operations at Landfill Cell B. The hydrogeological data, upgradient monitoring well detections (MW-11), CSIA results, and waste profile analysis all support this conclusion. Terravance recommends that:

> \(a\) SWMU-4 be excluded from GRS\'s corrective action scope under the Consent Decree, or, alternatively, GRS\'s remediation obligations at SWMU-4 be limited to conditions demonstrated to originate from GRS operations;
>
> \(b\) Additional investigation --- including the installation of at least two additional monitoring wells along the northeastern property boundary and expanded CSIA sampling --- be conducted to further define the relative contributions of GRS and Consolidated Metalworks to the vinyl chloride contamination at MW-12;
>
> \(c\) GRS preserve its contribution and cost-recovery rights under CERCLA Section 113(f) and applicable state law against Consolidated Metalworks and other potentially responsible parties associated with the Consolidated Metalworks NPL site; and
>
> \(d\) If SWMU-4 is excluded from GRS\'s remediation scope, the total estimated remediation cost would decrease from \$10,800,000 to approximately \$8,900,000.

**4. Combined Impact.** If both MNA is selected as the remedy at SWMU-3 and SWMU-4 is excluded from GRS\'s corrective action scope, the total estimated remediation cost would be approximately **\$6,000,000** (\$1,800,000 + \$2,400,000 + \$1,200,000 + \$0 + \$600,000 = \$6,000,000), compared to the current estimate of \$10,800,000 --- a reduction of approximately **\$4,800,000**. This reduction is significant and should inform the settlement discussions and the structuring of financial assurance obligations.

**5.** Terravance is available to present these findings to Illinois EPA, Clarendon Technical Services, and the Court as needed, including through testimony at any evidentiary hearing on the Consent Decree, and to participate in the development of the CMS upon its initiation.

**6.** The full RI report, submitted in draft to Illinois EPA on January 15, 2023, contains the complete data tables, soil boring logs, monitoring well construction details, laboratory analytical reports, geochemical evaluation, compound-specific isotope analysis results, and fate and transport modeling input parameters and results referenced in this summary memorandum. The full report should be reviewed in conjunction with this summary.
