**KESSLER, ANDRADE & YUN LLP** **Attorneys at Law** 55 E. Monroe Street, Suite 2400 Chicago, Illinois 60603 Telephone: (312) 555-8200 Facsimile: (312) 555-8201 www.kaylaw.com

**Margaret S. Andrade** Partner mandrade@kaylaw.com Direct: (312) 555-8217

September 20, 2024

Rachel A. Downing, Esq. Partner Hartwell, Brannigan & Locke LLP 150 N. Wacker Drive, Suite 3200 Chicago, Illinois 60606

> **cc:** Kevin M. Pratt, Esq., Senior Associate, Hartwell, Brannigan & Locke LLP (same address)
>
> **cc:** Martin J. Calloway, Deputy Bureau Chief, Environmental Bureau, Office of the Illinois Attorney General, 100 W. Randolph Street, Chicago, Illinois 60601

**Re:** *Fox River Conservancy v. Greenfield Recycling Solutions, Inc.*, Case No. 2021-CH-00847, Circuit Court of Winnebago County, Seventeenth Judicial Circuit --- FRC Settlement Demands and Position on Proposed Consent Decree

Dear Ms. Downing:

**[I. Introduction and Purpose]{.underline}**

This firm represents Fox River Conservancy (\"FRC\") in the above-captioned matter. We write to set forth FRC\'s settlement demands and to articulate FRC\'s position on the proposed Consent Decree circulated by the Office of the Illinois Attorney General (\"AG\") on September 8, 2024. We are transmitting this letter well in advance of the October 7, 2024 deadline for Greenfield Recycling Solutions, Inc. (\"GRS\") to return its markup so that GRS and its counsel are fully apprised of FRC\'s positions before finalizing any proposed revisions.

As you are aware, FRC filed its citizen-suit complaint on July 8, 2021, pursuant to Section 7002 of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (\"RCRA\"), 42 U.S.C. § 6972, and the Illinois Environmental Protection Act, 415 ILCS 5/1 *et seq*. FRC was granted intervenor status by the Honorable Patricia Sung on October 14, 2021. FRC is an Illinois not-for-profit corporation with approximately 2,300 members, a substantial number of whom reside within five miles of the GRS Rockford facility located at 4200 Industrial Corridor Drive, Rockford, Illinois 61101. FRC\'s Executive Director, Dr. Lena M. Okafor, and its members have a direct, personal, and continuing stake in the environmental conditions at and surrounding the GRS facility. FRC has participated actively in every phase of this litigation for more than three years---through pleadings, discovery, expert consultation, review of the Terravance Environmental Group draft Remedial Investigation (\"RI\") submitted January 15, 2023, and ongoing settlement negotiations---and maintains a substantial and direct interest in the remediation outcome.

FRC generally supports the framework of the proposed Consent Decree. The decree reflects many of the enforcement priorities FRC has advocated throughout this litigation. However, we write separately to emphasize provisions that FRC considers non-negotiable and to identify areas where FRC believes the decree must be strengthened rather than weakened. We are aware that GRS intends to submit a markup proposing revisions to the proposed Consent Decree, and we want FRC\'s positions to be unambiguous before any negotiations over that markup commence.

The factual record amply justifies a robust Consent Decree. Groundwater sampling has confirmed contamination in monitoring wells adjacent to tributary streams feeding the Rock River watershed. Trichloroethylene (\"TCE\") was detected at monitoring well MW-7 at a concentration of 28.4 µg/L and at MW-9 at 19.7 µg/L---levels that exceed the Class I groundwater quality standard of 5 µg/L established under 35 IAC 620.410 by factors of approximately 5.7 and 3.9, respectively. Chromium contamination in sediment at AOC-1 (Stormwater Outfall to Tributary) was measured at 210 mg/kg, indicating significant discharge of contaminants into the environment surrounding the facility. These are not marginal exceedances; they represent ongoing threats to public health and the ecological integrity of the Rock River corridor. The decree must be drafted and enforced accordingly.

**[II. FRC\'s Fee and Cost Recovery Demands]{.underline}**

FRC demands payment of its attorneys\' fees in the amount of Four Hundred Seventy-Five Thousand Dollars (\$475,000.00) and its technical consultant fees in the amount of One Hundred Twenty-Five Thousand Dollars (\$125,000.00), for a total demand of Six Hundred Thousand Dollars (\$600,000.00). This amount reflects more than three years of active litigation, including the preparation and filing of FRC\'s citizen-suit complaint, the contested motion for intervenor status, extensive participation in fact and expert discovery, thorough review and analysis of the Terravance draft RI, and ongoing settlement negotiations through multiple rounds of mediation. FRC\'s technical consultant reviewed all sampling data associated with Solid Waste Management Units 1 through 4 (\"SWMUs 1--4\") and AOC-1, prepared expert memoranda, and attended two full-day site inspections with Illinois EPA personnel.

The amount demanded is reasonable and well-supported. FRC maintains detailed contemporaneous billing records for both legal and consultant services, which are available for *in camera* review by the Court upon request. The fee demand is well within the range of reasonable citizen-suit fee awards under RCRA § 7002(e), 42 U.S.C. § 6972(e), and analogous provisions of the Illinois Environmental Protection Act. FRC considers this amount non-negotiable and expects it to be included in the final Consent Decree as a separate payment obligation of GRS, payable within sixty (60) days of entry of the decree.

**[III. Supplemental Environmental Project --- FRC Administration]{.underline}**

FRC strongly supports the proposed \$2.0 million Supplemental Environmental Project (\"SEP\") for wetlands restoration along the Rock River corridor as set forth in the proposed Consent Decree. The SEP represents a meaningful investment in restoring ecological function to habitats degraded by decades of contamination emanating from the GRS facility and surrounding industrial operations. However, FRC insists upon a condition that it considers essential to the success of the SEP: FRC must serve as the sole administrator of the SEP.

FRC\'s demand is grounded in the following considerations:

**Organizational Expertise.** FRC has administered wetlands restoration and riparian buffer projects in the Rock River watershed for more than fifteen years. Dr. Okafor holds a Ph.D. in environmental science from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, specializing in riparian ecology and wetland hydrology, and has directed over \$4.0 million in conservation projects funded through state grants, federal cooperative agreements, and private donations. FRC\'s staff includes two additional environmental scientists, a GIS specialist, and a full-time grants administrator. No third-party administrator or outside entity can match FRC\'s depth of experience in implementing precisely the type of project contemplated by the SEP. FRC is uniquely positioned to deliver maximum environmental benefit per dollar expended.

**Community Connection.** FRC\'s approximately 2,300 members are the direct beneficiaries of the wetlands restoration. They live, recreate, and work along the Rock River corridor. They fish in the tributaries that receive stormwater runoff from the GRS facility. FRC\'s administration of the SEP ensures that the project is accountable to the community most affected by the contamination---not to a distant bureaucracy or a consulting firm selected by the polluter itself. Community trust in the SEP\'s integrity and outcomes is essential, and that trust can only be achieved through FRC\'s stewardship.

**Efficiency and Cost-Effectiveness.** FRC maintains existing relationships with riparian landowners, local excavation and planting contractors, the Winnebago County Forest Preserve District, the Illinois Department of Natural Resources, and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. These relationships allow FRC to implement restoration projects more quickly, with lower overhead, and with greater ecological precision than a third-party administrator unfamiliar with local conditions, stakeholders, and regulatory requirements. Every dollar spent on duplicative administrative overhead is a dollar diverted from on-the-ground restoration.

**Full Administrative Authority.** FRC demands sole authority over all aspects of SEP implementation, including project design, contractor selection, fund disbursement, scheduling, and reporting. FRC will provide annual progress reports to Illinois EPA and to the Court, documenting expenditures, work completed, ecological outcomes, and projected future activities. This reporting framework provides all necessary transparency and accountability. FRC opposes any proposal for a \"joint oversight committee,\" an independent third-party administrator, or any other structure that would dilute FRC\'s administrative authority. Such arrangements invariably create bureaucratic delays, diffuse accountability, and undermine project effectiveness. FRC has seen this pattern in other environmental settlements and is determined to avoid it here.

**Audit and Financial Oversight.** FRC will comply with standard nonprofit accounting practices applicable to organizations of its size and type, including maintenance of separate accounts for SEP funds, preparation of annual financial statements, and submission to annual audits conducted by an independent certified public accountant. These measures provide robust financial accountability. FRC opposes, however, any provision granting GRS direct audit rights over SEP expenditures. GRS is the polluter. It is the entity whose violations of federal and state environmental law necessitated this enforcement action. It should not be granted veto authority, supervisory control, or investigative access over how remediation and restoration dollars are deployed. Any GRS audit right would function as a mechanism to second-guess legitimate project expenditures, delay implementation through protracted disputes over line items, and ultimately obstruct the very restoration the SEP is designed to achieve. The appropriate oversight bodies are Illinois EPA and the Court---not the respondent.

**Nexus to Contamination.** The wetlands restoration contemplated by the SEP has a direct and well-established nexus to the contamination at the GRS facility. AOC-1, the Stormwater Outfall to Tributary, has discharged chromium-laden sediment at concentrations of 210 mg/kg into downstream reaches of the Rock River watershed. This discharge has degraded wetland habitat, impaired water quality, and diminished ecological function in the corridor. The SEP is designed to remediate precisely these harms. FRC\'s administration ensures that the project is directed by an organization with intimate knowledge of the affected ecosystem and a demonstrated commitment to its restoration.

FRC considers its role as sole SEP administrator to be non-negotiable. Any proposal to substitute a third-party administrator, impose a joint oversight structure, or grant GRS audit authority over SEP funds will be opposed by FRC in the strongest terms.

**[IV. FRC Facility Access and Inspection Rights]{.underline}**

FRC demands unrestricted access to the GRS Rockford facility, including the right to conduct unannounced inspections, on terms equivalent to the access granted to Illinois EPA under Section 14.1 of the proposed Consent Decree.

**Statutory and Procedural Basis.** FRC\'s citizen-suit standing under RCRA § 7002 and the Illinois Environmental Protection Act confers upon FRC a continuing role in ensuring that GRS achieves and maintains compliance with environmental standards. FRC\'s intervenor status, granted on October 14, 2021, entitles it to full party rights in this action, including the right to participate in enforcement, monitoring, and oversight of the Consent Decree. Access to the facility is an inherent incident of FRC\'s party status and its continuing obligation to its members to verify that remediation is proceeding as required.

**GRS\'s Track Record of Non-Compliance.** GRS has a documented and troubling history of environmental violations at the Rockford facility. The Illinois EPA inspection conducted in March 2020 revealed widespread deficiencies in the storage and handling of hazardous waste, including improper management of F001--F005 listed wastes (spent halogenated and non-halogenated solvents), D008 characteristic wastes (lead-acid battery residues), and electronic waste leachate containing D006 (cadmium) and D007 (chromium). These violations were serious enough to warrant a Violation Notice issued June 15, 2020, followed by a formal Complaint and Compliance Order issued September 2, 2020. Given this track record, citizen oversight through direct facility access is not a luxury---it is a necessity.

**Scope of Access.** FRC demands the right to: (a) enter the GRS facility at any time during normal business hours without prior notice to GRS or its representatives; (b) inspect all SWMUs (1 through 4) and AOC-1, including all treatment, storage, and disposal areas, containment structures, and monitoring well locations; (c) collect split samples during any GRS or Illinois EPA monitoring event; (d) review all environmental records maintained on-site, including manifests, inspection logs, monitoring data, and correspondence with regulatory agencies; (e) photograph and document conditions observed during any inspection; and (f) bring FRC\'s technical consultants onto the facility to assist in inspections and sampling activities.

**Opposition to Proposed Limitations.** FRC specifically anticipates and rejects any proposal to limit FRC\'s oversight to periodic written reports or scheduled site visits. Quarterly reports are no substitute for direct observation. GRS\'s history of non-compliance demonstrates that paper reporting alone is insufficient to protect FRC\'s members and the environment. Contaminant releases can occur between reporting periods, and conditions documented in reports may not reflect actual site conditions. FRC similarly opposes any requirement that FRC site visits be accompanied by GRS representatives or preceded by advance notification. Such requirements would amount to an attempt to monitor the monitors---allowing GRS to prepare the facility before inspections and to control what FRC observes. Independent, unannounced access is essential to genuine oversight.

**Document Access.** FRC notes that Section 14.2 of the proposed Consent Decree requires GRS to provide Illinois EPA access to \"all documents, records, and communications, including attorney-client privileged materials, relating to contamination at or emanating from the Facility.\" FRC supports this provision and demands that any document access granted to Illinois EPA under the Consent Decree extend in full to FRC. There is no justification for providing the State with access to documents relevant to contamination while withholding those same documents from the citizen intervenor whose members bear the health and environmental consequences of that contamination.

FRC considers unrestricted facility access to be a non-negotiable element of any Consent Decree to which FRC will consent.

**[V. FRC\'s Position on Monitoring and Oversight]{.underline}**

FRC supports the thirty-year quarterly groundwater monitoring program (totaling 120 monitoring events) set forth in Section 12.4 of the proposed Consent Decree. The groundwater contamination at the GRS facility is extensive and well-documented: TCE at MW-7 at 28.4 µg/L, TCE at MW-9 at 19.7 µg/L, and vinyl chloride at MW-12 at 3.8 µg/L versus the applicable standard of 2.0 µg/L. These contaminant plumes affect the Rock River watershed and require sustained, long-term monitoring to confirm that corrective action has achieved and maintained compliance with applicable groundwater quality standards.

FRC opposes any \"adaptive\" or \"performance-based\" proposal to reduce monitoring frequency or to allow early termination of monitoring obligations. Such proposals are premature and scientifically unjustified given the extent and nature of contamination at the facility. GRS should not be permitted to declare victory after a few years of favorable readings. Contaminant rebound following initial treatment is a well-documented phenomenon in chlorinated solvent plumes, and only sustained, long-term data can confirm that groundwater remediation objectives have been durably achieved. FRC demands the right to receive copies of all monitoring reports within thirty (30) days of their completion, to attend all monitoring events, and to conduct its own independent monitoring at FRC\'s own expense, with GRS required to provide access to all monitoring wells for that purpose.

**[VI. FRC\'s Position on Remediation Scope and Covenant Not to Sue]{.underline}**

FRC supports the full scope of corrective action at all five areas identified in the proposed Consent Decree---SWMUs 1 through 4 and AOC-1---and opposes any attempt by GRS to narrow the corrective action scope or to attribute contamination to off-site sources as a basis for excluding any area from remediation.

FRC is aware that GRS may argue that vinyl chloride detected at SWMU-4 (MW-12, 3.8 µg/L) originates in whole or in part from the former Consolidated Metalworks facility at 4350 Industrial Corridor Drive, an NPL-listed site. FRC asserts that GRS bears the burden of demonstrating any off-site contribution, and that speculative allegations of third-party sourcing should not be permitted to delay or diminish corrective action at GRS\'s own facility. If GRS believes it has contribution claims against Consolidated Metalworks or its successors, it may pursue those claims independently; such claims are not a basis for weakening GRS\'s remediation obligations under the Consent Decree.

FRC likewise opposes any weakening of the covenant not to sue. The proposed Consent Decree appropriately conditions the covenant on GRS\'s achievement of all applicable remediation standards and completion of the full thirty-year monitoring program. GRS should not receive litigation peace until it has demonstrated sustained environmental compliance. FRC considers this structure non-negotiable and reserves the right to pursue additional claims should contamination prove more severe than currently characterized or should GRS fail to comply with its obligations under the decree.

**[VII. FRC\'s Position on Stipulated Penalties and Financial Assurance]{.underline}**

FRC supports the stipulated penalty structure set forth in the proposed Consent Decree: \$5,000 per day for days 1 through 30 of any violation, \$10,000 per day for days 31 through 60, and \$25,000 per day for day 61 and beyond, with no aggregate cap and no cure period. Strong stipulated penalties are the primary enforcement mechanism in consent decrees, and any dilution of the penalty structure undermines the decree\'s deterrent effect. A cure period would effectively give GRS a free pass for initial noncompliance, signaling that violations carry no immediate consequences. An aggregate cap would create a \"cost of doing business\" ceiling that permits GRS to calculate and budget for noncompliance. Neither is acceptable.

FRC supports the \$16.2 million financial assurance requirement, which represents 150% of estimated remediation costs. The 150% multiplier appropriately accounts for cost overruns, inflation, and the inherent uncertainty of environmental remediation projects that span decades. Given GRS\'s documented compliance failures, a robust financial assurance requirement is essential to ensuring that funds will be available to complete corrective action regardless of GRS\'s future financial condition. FRC opposes any reduction in the multiplier or extension of the posting deadline beyond that set forth in the proposed Consent Decree. FRC further demands that a portion of any stipulated penalties collected be directed to FRC for additional environmental monitoring and community outreach activities within the Rock River watershed.

**[VIII. Summary of FRC\'s Non-Negotiable Demands]{.underline}**

For clarity, FRC summarizes its non-negotiable positions as follows:

1\. Payment of \$600,000 (\$475,000 in attorneys\' fees and \$125,000 in technical consultant fees) to FRC, payable within sixty (60) days of entry of the Consent Decree.

2\. FRC sole administration of the \$2.0 million Supplemental Environmental Project for wetlands restoration, with full authority over project design, contractor selection, fund disbursement, and reporting, and without GRS audit rights or a joint oversight committee.

3\. Unrestricted FRC facility access equivalent to Illinois EPA\'s access under Section 14.1, including unannounced inspections during business hours, independent split sampling, and unrestricted document review.

4\. Full thirty-year quarterly groundwater monitoring program with no adaptive reductions in frequency and no early termination provisions.

5\. No exclusion of SWMU-4 from the corrective action scope, regardless of any alleged off-site contribution.

6\. Covenant not to sue conditioned on GRS\'s completion of all remediation obligations and the full thirty-year monitoring program.

7\. Uncapped stipulated penalties at the rates specified in the proposed Consent Decree, with no cure period.

8\. Full document access, including attorney-client privileged materials relating to contamination, on terms equivalent to those extended to Illinois EPA.

FRC considers each of these positions to be non-negotiable. If GRS\'s markup materially weakens any of these provisions, FRC will oppose entry of the Consent Decree, will seek to continue the litigation on its citizen-suit claims, and will move for summary judgment on liability. FRC\'s claims under RCRA § 7002 and the Illinois Environmental Protection Act are independent of the State\'s enforcement action. FRC is prepared to try this case if a satisfactory resolution cannot be reached.

**[IX. Closing]{.underline}**

FRC looks forward to reviewing GRS\'s markup of the proposed Consent Decree and to reaching a resolution that adequately protects the environment, the Rock River watershed, and FRC\'s members. We note the October 7, 2024 deadline for GRS to return the markup to the AG\'s office and respectfully request that Hartwell, Brannigan & Locke LLP provide a courtesy copy of the markup to this office simultaneously with its submission to the AG\'s office. Prompt disclosure will facilitate an efficient review process and, we hope, expeditious resolution of any remaining disputes.

We are available to discuss any of the matters addressed in this letter at your convenience.

Respectfully submitted,

KESSLER, ANDRADE & YUN LLP

import sys
import zipfile
from pathlib import Path
from lxml import etree


def validate(path: Path) -> list[str]:
    errors = []

    if not path.exists():
        return [f"File not found: {path}"]
    if not zipfile.is_zipfile(path):
        return [f"Not a valid ZIP: {path}"]

    with zipfile.ZipFile(path) as z:
        names = set(z.namelist())

        if "[Content_Types].xml" not in names:
            errors.append("Missing [Content_Types].xml")
            return errors

        # XML well-formedness for every .xml and .rels part
        for name in names:
            if name.endswith(".xml") or name.endswith(".rels"):
                try:
                    etree.fromstring(z.read(name))
                except etree.XMLSyntaxError as e:
                    errors.append(f"Malformed XML in {name}: {e}")

        # Relationship target consistency
        for rels_name in [n for n in names if n.endswith(".rels")]:
            try:
                rels = etree.fromstring(z.read(rels_name))
            except etree.XMLSyntaxError:
                continue
            ns = "{http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/package/2006/relationships}"
            for rel in rels.findall(f"{ns}Relationship"):
                target = rel.get("Target") or ""
                target_mode = rel.get("TargetMode", "Internal")
                if target_mode == "External" or target.startswith(("http", "mailto:")):

  c="[GRS Comment 1 — General] GRS wants to resolve this matter by consent decree and accepts the core economic terms of the AG draft, including the $3,750,000 civil penalty, the $2,000,000 SEP amount, the $600,000 FRC payment, the 12-month CMS schedule, and quarterly monitoring during active remediation. Our revisions are limited to provisions that (i) are not financially feasible on the timetable proposed, (ii) would deny GRS any meaningful finality, (iii) would make GRS responsible for contamination that the RI attributes to an off-site NPL source, or (iv) depart from standard Illinois and U.S. EPA consent decree practice. Each change is explained in a margin comment.", before=True)

# ---- Recitals
R("The investigation of the Facility, including a Remedial Investigation", "has identified contamination requiring corrective action at the following", "has identified the following conditions, which are to be addressed as provided in Section VII, at the following",
  c="[GRS Comment 2 — Recitals 7–9 / Section 5.1] As drafted, Section 5.1 would have GRS admit every Recital, including Clarendon`s conclusions (Recital 8) and the characterization of all five areas as GRS contamination \"requiring corrective action.\" The RI is still in draft and its findings on SWMU-3 (remedy) and SWMU-4 (source) are disputed. R("The applicable residential remediation objective for lead", "The applicable residential remediation objective for lead under 35 IAC 742 is 400 mg/kg.", "The Tier 1 residential remediation objective for lead under 35 IAC 742 is 400 mg/kg; the remediation objectives applicable to the Facility, which is in current and reasonably anticipated industrial/commercial use, will be determined under 35 IAC 742 in the CMS.",
  c="[GRS Comment 3 — Remediation Objectives] The RI compares results to the most conservative Tier 1 residential values (RI Table 1, n.2) and expressly contemplates site-specific objectives in the CMS. R("Tetrachloroethylene (\"PCE\") has been detected in soil", "exceeding the applicable remediation objective of 0.46 mg/kg", "exceeding the Tier 1 residential remediation objective of 0.46 mg/kg")
I("Vinyl chloride has been detected in groundwater at monitoring well MW-12", None, " The Remedial Investigation identifies the former Consolidated Metalworks facility at 4350 Industrial Corridor Drive, Rockford, Illinois, a site on the CERCLA National Priorities List located hydraulically upgradient of SWMU-4, as a likely source, in whole or in part, of the vinyl chloride detected at MW-12, based on, among other things, chlorinated ethenes detected at upgradient monitoring well MW-11, the documented northeast-to-southwest groundwater flow direction, the absence of chlorinated solvents in the Landfill Cell B waste profile, and compound-specific isotope analysis (RI Appendix H).",
  c="[GRS Comment 4 — SWMU-4] The RI documents (i) TCE (7.2 µg/L) and cis-1,2-DCE (12.5 µg/L) at MW-11, between the Consolidated Metalworks NPL site and Landfill Cell B; (ii) groundwater flow from that site toward SWMU-4; (iii) no chlorinated solvent waste streams in the Landfill Cell B records; and (iv) CSIA results more consistent with degradation of industrial TCE than with landfill-derived vinyl chloride. Clarendon has not done any upgradient source evaluation. The Recitals should reflect this record. See new Section 7.8.")
R("Chromium has been detected in sediment at a concentration of 210 mg/kg", "indicating releases from the Facility to the adjacent tributary stream.", "which is elevated relative to upstream background concentrations of 22 to 38 mg/kg; no promulgated remediation objective for chromium in sediment applies under 35 IAC 742.")
I("Clarendon Technical Services, Inc. (\"Clarendon\"), environmental consultant to the State, has reviewed", None, " GRS and its consultant, Terravance, do not concur in Clarendon`s attribution of the vinyl chloride detected at SWMU-4 to GRS operations or in Clarendon`s position that active pump-and-treat remediation is required at SWMU-3; these matters are to be resolved as provided in Sections VII and XVII.")
R("The total estimated cost of the remediation necessary", "These cost estimates are based upon the assumption that active remediation technologies will be employed at all SWMUs and AOCs and include", "These cost estimates are order-of-magnitude planning estimates that assume active remediation technologies will be employed at all SWMUs and AOCs (including pump-and-treat at SWMU-3 and groundwater extraction and treatment at SWMU-4), are subject to refinement in the CMS, and include",
  c="[GRS Comment 5 — Recital 9] The $10.8 million figure is the RI`s order-of-magnitude estimate under Clarendon`s presumptive remedies. defs = [
 ("2.18", "\"Consolidated Metalworks Site\" means the former Consolidated Metalworks facility located at 4350 Industrial Corridor Drive, Rockford, Illinois, which is listed on the National Priorities List under CERCLA, together with all areas to which hazardous substances released at or from that facility have come to be located."),

]
first = True

  "The SEP shall be implemented by an independent, qualified SEP Administrator (such as a conservation organization, land trust, or public entity with demonstrated wetlands restoration experience) that is not a Party, selected by Illinois EPA after consultation with GRS and FRC, under a SEP Work Plan and budget approved by Illinois EPA. p97 = P(p96, [("9.7", B), (" ", N), ("Waiver.", It), (" The State may, in its unreviewable discretion, reduce or waive stipulated penalties otherwise due under this Section.", N)])

  c="[GRS Comment 20 — New Section IX-A] The AG draft has no force majeure clause, which is unusual for a decree that will run for many years.  ("9A.1", "Definition.", " \"Force Majeure\" means any event arising from causes beyond the control of GRS, its contractors, or any entity controlled by GRS that delays or prevents the performance of any obligation under this Consent Decree despite GRS`s best efforts to fulfill the obligation, including, without limitation: natural disasters, floods, extreme weather that prevents field work, fire, epidemic, war, civil disturbance, or labor disputes not involving GRS employees; unavailability of equipment, materials, or qualified contractors resulting from supply-chain disruptions not caused by GRS; delays in obtaining any permit, access agreement, or approval required from a governmental authority or third party, despite GRS`s timely and complete application and diligent efforts; changes in applicable law or regulation that materially affect the Work; and the discovery of subsurface conditions materially different from those described in the Remedial Investigation that could not reasonably have been anticipated. \"Best efforts\" includes using best efforts to anticipate any potential Force Majeure event and to address its effects as it is occurring and after it has occurred, so as to minimize delay to the greatest extent possible."),
 ("9A.2", "Exclusions.", " Force Majeure does not include increased cost or expense of performance, changed financial circumstances, or financial inability to perform, or the failure of GRS`s contractors to perform unless that failure itself results from a Force Majeure event."),
 ("9A.3", "Notice.", " GRS shall notify Illinois EPA (with a copy to FRC) orally or by email within five (5) Business Days, and in writing within ten (10) Business Days, after GRS first knew or should have known that an event may cause a Force Majeure delay.  ("9A.4", "Extension.", " If Illinois EPA agrees that the delay or anticipated delay is attributable to Force Majeure, the time for performance of the affected obligations shall be extended for such period as is necessary to complete those obligations, and no stipulated penalties shall accrue for the period of the extension. Illinois EPA shall notify GRS in writing of its decision within twenty (20) Business Days of receipt of GRS`s written notice."),
 ("9A.5", "Disputes.", " If Illinois EPA does not agree that a Force Majeure event has occurred, or disagrees with the length of the extension requested, GRS may invoke dispute resolution under Section XV. ]
last = h
for num, head, body in fm:
    last = P(last, [(num, B), (" ", N), (head, It), (body, N)], template=Q("Applicability. Stipulated penalties shall apply to each and every requirement"))
PYEOF

  "GRS shall establish and maintain financial assurance in an amount equal to one hundred twenty percent (120%) of the estimated cost of the corrective action required under Section VII (the \"Financial Assurance Amount\"), as follows: (a) within one hundred twenty (120) days of the Effective Date, GRS shall establish financial assurance in the initial amount of Six Million Four Hundred Eighty Thousand Dollars ($6,480,000), which is fifty percent (50%) of 120% of the total estimated cost of corrective action set forth in Recital 9 ($10,800,000 × 1.20 = $12,960,000; $12,960,000 × 0.50 = $6,480,000); and (b) within sixty (60) days after Illinois EPA`s approval of the CMS, and in no event later than twenty-one (21) months after the Effective Date, GRS shall increase the financial assurance to the full Financial Assurance Amount, calculated as 120% of the estimated cost of the Selected Remedies set forth in the approved CMS (plus the estimated cost of any remaining Work under Section 7.8).",
  c="[GRS Comment 21 — Section 11.1] GRS will post financial assurance. As drafted, though, Section 11.1 cannot be met. (1) Multiplier: 150% is well above the RCRA Subpart H baseline, which ties financial assurance to the cost estimate itself (35 IAC 724.243; 40 C.F.R. § 264.143) with annual adjustment. 120% gives a substantial contingency cushion and is the more common figure in Illinois decrees. Posting the full amount against an estimate that may fall by $2.9 to $4.8 million ties up credit for no environmental benefit. (3) Timing: no instrument can realistically be arranged in 60 days. GRS proposes 50% at 120 days and the balance, sized to the Selected Remedies, within 60 days of CMS approval, with an outside date of 21 months. Under this schedule the State holds financial assurance before any remedy construction begins.")

# ---- Section XIV Access
A = "Facility Access. GRS shall provide the State, Illinois EPA, FRC"
R(A, "GRS shall provide the State, Illinois EPA, FRC, and their respective agents", "GRS shall provide the State, Illinois EPA, and their respective agents",
  c="[GRS Comment 24 — Section 14.1] The State`s and Illinois EPA`s access rights are unchanged except for the ordinary condition of compliance with site health and safety rules on an active waste-processing facility. FRC`s rights are reframed. RCRA § 7002 gives a citizen plaintiff no inspection authority, and unannounced, unescorted access by an adverse litigant and its consultants at an operating RCRA facility raises safety, liability, and confidentiality concerns. FRC instead receives every progress and monitoring report, an annual escorted site visit on 10 Business Days` notice (more with Illinois EPA approval for good cause), and the right to observe and split-sample scheduled monitoring events at its own expense.")
R("GRS shall not require advance notice as a condition of such access", "GRS shall not require advance notice as a condition of such access and shall not impose any conditions, restrictions, or limitations on the access rights granted herein.", "GRS shall not require advance notice as a condition of access by the State or Illinois EPA and shall not impose any conditions, restrictions, or limitations on such access other than compliance with the Facility`s generally applicable health and safety requirements.")
R("FRC shall have the same access rights as Illinois EPA under this Section", "FRC shall have the same access rights as Illinois EPA under this Section, including but not limited to the right to conduct independent inspections and sampling of the Facility and its environs without prior coordination with or approval by GRS or Illinois EPA, and to retain and direct its own consultants and contractors for such purposes.",
  "FRC and its consultants shall be entitled to: (a) one (1) site visit per calendar year, and such additional visits as Illinois EPA may approve for good cause, on not less than ten (10) Business Days` written notice to GRS, during normal business hours, accompanied by GRS personnel, and subject to the Facility`s health and safety requirements; (b) copies of all progress reports and monitoring reports submitted to Illinois EPA under Sections 7.6 and 12.5; and (c) on reasonable advance notice, the opportunity to observe, and to collect split samples during, scheduled groundwater monitoring events under Section XII, at FRC`s own expense, with all FRC split-sample results provided to GRS and Illinois EPA.")
R("Document Access. GRS shall provide Illinois EPA and FRC, upon written or oral request", "GRS shall provide Illinois EPA and FRC, upon written or oral request, access to and copies of all documents", "GRS shall provide Illinois EPA, upon written or oral request (and FRC, upon written request, with respect to sampling and monitoring data, reports and submissions under this Consent Decree, and other non-privileged environmental records), access to and copies of all documents",
  c="[GRS Comment 25 — Section 14.2] A blanket waiver of attorney-client privilege and work product, running for the life of the Decree plus five years, is not found in Illinois or U.S. EPA model decrees, and no regulated party could sign it. GRS agrees that all sampling, analytical, monitoring, and other technical data, and every required submission, will be produced without any privilege claim. R("Document Access. GRS shall provide Illinois EPA", ", including materials protected by the attorney-client privilege, the work product doctrine, and any other applicable privilege or protection,", "")
R("GRS hereby waives any claim of attorney-client privilege", "GRS hereby waives any claim of attorney-client privilege, work product protection, or any other privilege, protection, or immunity with respect to such materials in connection with this Consent Decree and the matters addressed herein.   "GRS may withhold documents protected by the attorney-client privilege, the attorney work-product doctrine, or any other privilege or protection recognized under applicable law, provided that GRS provides a privilege log identifying, for each document withheld, its date, author, recipients, general subject matter, and the privilege asserted. I("Continued Compliance. R("Burden of Proof and Standard of Review.", "On any issue of interpretation of this Consent Decree, the State`s reasonable interpretation shall be given deference, and the Court shall adopt the State`s interpretation unless GRS demonstrates that the State`s interpretation is plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the express terms of this Decree.",
  "In any dispute concerning the selection or adequacy of a remedy or other technical determination by Illinois EPA under Sections VII, XI, or XII, the Court shall review Illinois EPA`s determination on the administrative record and shall uphold it unless it is arbitrary and capricious or otherwise not in accordance with law. Disputes concerning the interpretation of this Consent Decree shall be resolved by the Court de novo, applying ordinary principles of contract interpretation.",
  c="[GRS Comment 26 — Section 15.4] A consent decree is construed as a contract. GRS proposes the conventional split: deferential record review of Illinois EPA`s technical determinations, and de novo review of contract interpretation.")

# ---- Section XVII Covenant
R("State`s Covenant.   "the State of Illinois covenants not to bring any civil judicial or administrative action against GRS with respect to the Matters Addressed, including any claims arising from the same operative facts alleged in the State`s Complaint filed April 22, 2021, in Case No. 2021-CH-00847, as follows:",
  c="[GRS Comment 27 — Section XVII (Covenant Not to Sue)] As drafted, the covenant takes effect only after GRS has met every cleanup standard and finished 30 years of monitoring. GRS proposes the phased structure used in U.S. EPA model decrees. Civil penalty claims are released on the Effective Date. Injunctive and corrective action claims are released upon Remedy Completion. Long-term monitoring continues as an independent obligation and is not a condition of the covenant. The State`s position remains fully protected: the covenant is conditioned on performance, Sections 17.3 and XVIII preserve the reservations and reopeners, and the State keeps full power to enforce the Decree.")

  [("Injunctive Relief and Corrective Action Claims.", It), (" Effective upon Remedy Completion, the State covenants not to sue or take administrative action against GRS for injunctive relief, corrective action, or response costs with respect to the Matters Addressed, other than to enforce this Consent Decree, subject to Section XVIII. R("GRS has satisfied all other obligations under this Consent Decree, including but not limited to the payment of all civil penalties, stipulated penalties, FRC payments, and SEP funding",
  "GRS has satisfied all other obligations under this Consent Decree, including but not limited to the payment of all civil penalties, stipulated penalties, FRC payments, and SEP funding, the completion of all corrective action required under Section VII, and the establishment and maintenance of financial assurance under Section XI.",
  [("Remedy Completion; Continuing Obligations.", It), (" When GRS believes that Remedy Completion has occurred, it shall submit a Remedy Completion Report to Illinois EPA and FRC. Within ninety (90) days of receipt, Illinois EPA shall either issue a written certification of Remedy Completion or explain in writing the deficiencies and the actions required to achieve Remedy Completion; disputes are subject to Section XV. The covenants in this Section are conditioned upon GRS`s continued performance of its obligations under this Consent Decree. GRS`s monitoring, reporting, financial assurance, and record-keeping obligations under Sections XI, XII, and XIII shall survive Remedy Completion and are not conditions precedent to the effectiveness of the covenants in this Section.", N)])
R("FRC`s Covenant. Subject to the conditions and limitations set forth in Section 17.3 below", "provided, however, that this covenant shall not become effective until each of the conditions set forth in Section 17.1(a)–(c) has been fully and completely satisfied.",
  "which covenant shall become effective as to civil penalty claims upon the Effective Date, and as to claims for injunctive relief, corrective action, or response costs upon Remedy Completion, on the same terms and conditions as set forth in Section 17.1(a)–(c).")
R("No Third-Party Rights. This Consent Decree does not create any rights", "Nothing in this Consent Decree shall be construed as providing any protection to GRS against claims brought by any person or entity not a party to this Consent Decree, including but not limited to claims for contribution, cost recovery, property damage, or personal injury.",
  "Except as provided in Section 17.5, nothing in this Consent Decree shall be construed as providing any protection to GRS against claims brought by any person or entity not a party to this Consent Decree, including claims for property damage or personal injury.")
p174 = D.find(Q("No Third-Party Rights. This Consent Decree does not create any rights"))
p175 = P(p174, [("17.5", B), (" ", N), ("Contribution Protection and Reservation of GRS Rights.", It), (" (a) The Parties agree, and by entering this Consent Decree the Court finds, that this Consent Decree is a judicially approved settlement under which GRS has resolved its liability to the State for the Matters Addressed within the meaning of Section 113(f)(2) of CERCLA, 42 U.S.C. § 9613(f)(2), and that, as of the Effective Date, GRS is entitled to protection from contribution actions or claims for the Matters Addressed as provided by Section 113(f)(2) of CERCLA and, to the fullest extent permitted by law, by applicable Illinois law, including 740 ILCS 100/2. (b) Nothing in this Consent Decree waives, releases, or impairs any claim, right, or cause of action of GRS against any person not a Party to this Consent Decree, including the owners or operators (past or present) of the Consolidated Metalworks Site, their successors, any other potentially responsible party for that site, or the United States, for contribution, cost recovery, indemnity, or other relief under Sections 107 and 113(f) of CERCLA, 42 U.S.C. §§ 9607 and 9613(f), Section 22.2(f) of the Illinois Environmental Protection Act, 415 ILCS 5/22.2(f), or other applicable law, with respect to costs incurred or to be incurred in connection with the Facility, including SWMU-4. (c) Amounts expended by GRS under this Consent Decree are \"response costs\" incurred consistent with the National Contingency Plan, 40 C.F.R. Part 300, to the extent permitted by law.", N)],
  c="[GRS Comment 28 — New Section 17.5] GRS is paying for corrective action under State supervision and should have the contribution protection customarily given to a settling party for the Matters Addressed. # ---- Section XVIII Reopener
R("General Reopener. The State may reopen this Consent Decree and require GRS to perform additional work", "The State may reopen this Consent Decree and require GRS to perform additional work, provide additional financial assurance, pay additional penalties, or take such other actions as the State deems appropriate, if any of the following conditions is found to exist:",
  "The State may petition the Court under Section 18.3 to modify this Consent Decree to require GRS to perform additional corrective action (and to provide corresponding financial assurance) if any of the following conditions is found to exist and that condition or information, together with any other relevant information, indicates that the corrective action required under this Consent Decree is not protective of human health or the environment:",
  c="[GRS Comment 29 — Section XVIII] The reopener has been conformed to the U.S. EPA model unknown-conditions/new-information formulation. Reopening requires (i) conditions or information previously unknown and not reasonably available when the Decree was lodged, (ii) a causal connection to releases from GRS`s operations rather than off-site migration, (iii) materiality, and (iv) a showing that the remedy is not protective. A reopener should not be a route to new penalties or to work unrelated to new conditions. Pp("Your email describes the Pinnacle Indemnity pollution legal liability policy (No. PIG-ENV-2019-04227; $5M limit; $500K SIR) as worthless because of the known-conditions exclusion. The exclusion reaches conditions known before the April 1, 2019 inception. The violations were first identified at the March 2020 inspection, and the RI dates the SWMU-3 spills to 2011–2016, so the question will be what GRS knew before April 2019. That is a disputed fact question, not a foregone conclusion. Two consequences follow. (1) The markup narrows GRS`s admissions in Section 5.1 to Recitals 1–6 (Comment 2), partly so the decree cannot be used as an admission of pre-inception knowledge. (2) Coverage counsel should confirm that notice and tender are complete and should manage the April 1, 2025 renewal. A recovery would help fund remediation. A compliant policy written under 35 IAC 724.243(e) could also serve as a financial assurance mechanism under revised Section 11.3.", align="j")

Pp("The AG draft`s Appendix D would attach the \"Remedial Investigation Summary (Draft Dated January 15, 2023), Prepared by Terravance.\" Dr. Sheffield`s January 15, 2023 Technical Memorandum to Sandra and you carries exactly that description, is marked privileged and prepared at the direction of counsel, and contains statements helpful to the other side. Examples: SWMU-1, SWMU-2 and AOC-1 are \"clearly attributable to GRS operations\"; SWMU-3 contamination \"is attributable to GRS operations\"; and the SWMU-3 spill history for 2011–2016. We need to confirm immediately whether the AG has the memorandum (inadvertent production would call for a clawback under Ill. S. Ct. R. 201(p)) or is simply using imprecise shorthand for the RI Report. For the same reason, the revised privilege provision (Section 14.2) protects consultant communications made at the direction of counsel.", align="j")
H("H. Technical vulnerabilities in the Terravance analysis (for Dr. Sheffield before October 7)", 2)
for b in [
 "**MW-13 versus the off-site source theory (most significant).** RI Table 2 places background well MW-13 at the \"northeast perimeter of the Facility upgradient of all SWMUs,\" non-detect for TCE and all VOCs. Note 4 says this confirms that groundwater is not VOC-impacted \"in the absence of a local source.\" The Consolidated Metalworks site lies to the northeast. Clarendon will argue that an off-site plume entering from the northeast should appear at MW-13. Dr. Sheffield needs to explain the plume geometry (for example, that MW-13 lies outside the plume`s flow path and that MW-11 lies inside it) with maps, ideally from RI Appendix E/F.",
 "**MNA timeframe.** The modeling uses a TCE half-life of about 2.8 years. The observed declines imply slower attenuation at MW-7: 42.1 → 28.4 µg/L over about 2.75 years is a half-life of about **4.8 years**, which projects attainment of 5 µg/L in about **12 years**, not 8–10. MW-9 implies about 4.0 years and about 8 years. The $1.2M MNA cost assumes 10 years of monitoring. Clarendon will make this point. The CMS should present a range, and the cost estimate should be sensitivity-tested.",
 "**Seepage velocity.** The stated inputs (K = 3.2 × 10⁻³ cm/s, i = 0.008, nₑ = 0.25) yield about **106 ft/yr**, not the 75 ft/yr reported. Ask Dr. Sheffield to reconcile; it affects plume travel time and BIOSCREEN outputs.",
 "**Landfill Cell B waste profile.** The RI states the cell received C&D debris and \"certain industrial wastes\" and \"limited quantities of non-hazardous industrial waste from GRS`s recycling operations.\" Those operations managed F001–F005 solvents. The \"no solvents in Cell B\" premise needs record support (manifests and operating logs), and that is why Section 7.8(c) includes a records review.",
 "**Data currency.** RI groundwater data run through December 2022.  "**Minor.** The RI text identifies MW-1/MW-2 as downgradient of SWMU-1, while Table 2 lists MW-5. MW-11 is described as \"75 feet northeast of the GRS property boundary,\" which suggests it sits off-site, and we should confirm the access arrangement.",
 "**EPA Region 5 record.** The Consolidated Metalworks site is on the NPL. Pulling it is quick and inexpensive, and it would be the most persuasive support we could cite to Calloway.",
]: Bl(b)
H("I. CERCLA contribution mechanics (Section 17.5)", 2)
Pp("Section 17.5 (Comment 28) seeks contribution protection under CERCLA § 113(f)(2) and preserves GRS`s claims against Consolidated Metalworks and other PRPs under CERCLA §§ 107 and 113(f) and 415 ILCS 5/22.2(f). Three cautions follow.", align="j")
for b in [
 "Under __Territory of Guam v. United States__, 593 U.S. 310 (2021), a § 113(f)(3)(B) contribution claim arises only from a settlement that resolves CERCLA-specific liability. The State`s complaint pleads the Illinois Act and RCRA, not CERCLA. A recital that the decree is a § 113(f)(2) settlement may not by itself create CERCLA contribution protection or a § 113(f)(3)(B) claim. One option is to ask the AG to add a CERCLA § 107 claim (or state-law cost recovery under 415 ILCS 5/22.2(f)) to the matters resolved. That makes protection more robust, but it also triggers points 2 and 3.",
 "If the decree **does** qualify as a CERCLA settlement, the **three-year limitations period** for GRS`s contribution claim under § 113(g)(3)(B) runs from entry. We must calendar it, and we should consider sending a tolling request to the Consolidated Metalworks PRPs promptly.",
 "If it does **not** qualify, GRS likely retains a § 107(a) cost-recovery claim (__United States v. Atlantic Research Corp.__, 551 U.S. 128 (2007)) for costs it incurs, which carries a different limitations period and the potential for joint-and-several recovery. Section 17.5(b) is drafted to preserve both routes, and Section 17.5(c) characterizes GRS`s expenditures as NCP-consistent response costs to support recovery. Recommendation: hold the CERCLA-claim question for the first AG call. Either way, the reservation of rights in Section 17.5(b) is the non-negotiable piece.",
]: Bl(b, num=False)

Pp("Section 17.5 (Comment 28) seeks contribution protection under CERCLA § 113(f)(2) and preserves GRS`s claims against Consolidated Metalworks and other PRPs under CERCLA §§ 107 and 113(f) and 415 ILCS 5/22.2(f). Three cautions follow.", align="j")
for b in [
 "Under __Territory of Guam v. United States__, 593 U.S. 310 (2021), a § 113(f)(3)(B) contribution claim arises only from a settlement that resolves CERCLA-specific liability. The State`s complaint pleads the Illinois Act and RCRA, not CERCLA. A recital that the decree is a § 113(f)(2) settlement may not by itself create CERCLA contribution protection or a § 113(f)(3)(B) claim. One option is to ask the AG to add a CERCLA § 107 claim (or state-law cost recovery under 415 ILCS 5/22.2(f)) to the matters resolved. That makes protection more robust, but it also triggers points 2 and 3.",
 "If the decree **does** qualify as a CERCLA settlement, the **three-year limitations period** for GRS`s contribution claim under § 113(g)(3)(B) runs from entry. We must calendar it, and we should consider sending a tolling request to the Consolidated Metalworks PRPs promptly.",
 "If it does **not** qualify, GRS likely retains a § 107(a) cost-recovery claim (__United States v. Atlantic Research Corp.__, 551 U.S. 128 (2007)) for costs it incurs, which carries a different limitations period and the potential for joint-and-several recovery. Section 17.5(b) is drafted to preserve both routes, and Section 17.5(c) characterizes GRS`s expenditures as NCP-consistent response costs to support recovery. Recommendation: hold the CERCLA-claim question for the first AG call. Either way, the reservation of rights in Section 17.5(b) is the non-negotiable piece.",

**PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL --- ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT**

**HARTWELL, BRANNIGAN & LOCKE LLP**

**MEMORANDUM**

  ----------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **TO:**                             Rachel A. Downing, Partner

  **FROM:**                           Kevin M. Pratt, Senior Associate

  **DATE:**                           September 30, 2024

  **RE:**                             *People of the State of Illinois, ex rel. Attorney General, and Fox River Conservancy v. Greenfield Recycling Solutions, Inc.*, Case No. 2021-CH-00847 (Cir. Ct. Winnebago Cnty.) (Sung, J.) --- Cover memorandum to GRS redline of the AG's September 8, 2024 proposed Consent Decree: summary of revisions, rationale, risk assessment, open items, and fallback positions
  ----------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Deliverables.** (1) consent-decree-markup.docx: tracked-changes redline of the September 8 AG draft, with 33 numbered margin comments (\[GRS Comment 1\]--\[GRS Comment 33\]) explaining each revision. The comments are written to be read by Calloway's office and Andrade, but see the transmittal checklist in Part IX before the redline leaves the firm. (2) This memorandum, which is internal only. Return deadline to the AG is **October 7, 2024**. Your review is blocked for October 1.

# I. Bottom Line

- Per your direction, the markup is targeted and not a rewrite. It contains roughly 70 discrete tracked revisions across 20 sections, plus one new section (IX-A, Force Majeure) and two new subsections (7.8, SWMU-4; 17.5, contribution protection and reservation of rights). Every economic term you told me to leave alone is untouched: the \$3.75M penalty, the \$2.0M SEP amount, the \$600K FRC payment, the 12-month CMS, and quarterly monitoring during remediation.

- **Tier 1 (dealbreakers):** (a) financial assurance and payment timing (Sections 6.1, 8.3, 11.1--11.4); (b) a phased covenant not to sue (Section XVII); (c) SWMU-4 handled through Option A, a source evaluation before any corrective action obligation, together with an express reservation of GRS's contribution and cost-recovery rights (Sections 7.7, 7.8, 17.5).

- **The liquidity problem is worse than our working numbers.** Including the SEP (\$2.0M) and the FRC payment (\$0.6M), which are also due within 60 days, the AG draft demands **\$20.3M within 60 days**, not \$17.7M. The 120% / 120-day counter in your email still breaches the Beacon \$5M minimum-liquidity covenant, and it cannot be posted as a single letter of credit because \$12.96M is more than both the \$12.7M of revolver availability and the \$10M LC sub-limit. The markup therefore stages financial assurance: 50% at 120 days, and the balance sized to the remedies actually selected, posted 60 days after CMS approval (outside date 21 months). On the workbook's own assumptions, that structure keeps GRS above the covenant (Part III).

- **The financial test and corporate guarantee are probably not available to GRS today.** On the June 30, 2024 balance sheet, GRS fails the 35 IAC 724.243(f) / 40 C.F.R. § 264.143(f) criteria by a wide margin (Part II.C). The markup still asks for these mechanisms because they cost nothing to include and preserve future flexibility. The liquidity plan, however, cannot depend on them, and we should correct the workbook's statement that the financial test is the strongest outcome.

- **Two items need to be fixed before anything goes out.** (1) Decree Appendix D, as drafted by the AG, would attach the Terravance \"Remedial Investigation Summary (Draft Dated January 15, 2023).\" The only document by that description in our file is Dr. Sheffield's privileged technical memorandum prepared at the direction of counsel. The markup substitutes the RI Report as submitted to Illinois EPA (Comment 33). We need to confirm what the AG actually has. (2) The GRS financial workbook contains internal errors (Part II.E) that must be corrected before any ability-to-pay information goes to the AG.

- **Expected reception.** The AG is likely to accept, with negotiation, the privilege carve-out, force majeure, the 162(f) language, the TACO/ROs conforming changes, the MNA-in-the-CMS requirement, and payment timing. Hard negotiation is likely on the financial assurance multiplier and staging, the covenant, the stipulated-penalty cap, the reopener, and SWMU-4. FRC's September 20 letter labels as \"non-negotiable\" seven of the eight positions our markup touches; the only one we accept outright is its fee demand. Part VI addresses how to manage FRC.

# II. Issues to Resolve Before Transmittal (Corrections to Working Assumptions)

## A. Near-term cash demand under the AG draft is \$20.3M, not \$17.7M

The direction email and the workbook (Balance Sheet tab and Credit Facility tab) count only the \$1.5M first penalty installment (30 days) and the \$16.2M of financial assurance (60 days). The draft also requires the full \$2.0M SEP transfer within 60 days (Section 8.3) and the \$600K FRC payment within 60 days (Sections 10.1--10.2). The workbook's 24-month model instead assumes the SEP is paid in tranches beginning at month 12 and the FRC payment at month 6, which is not what the draft says. The corrected 60-day demand is **\$20.3M** against **\$15.55M** of total liquidity (cash of \$2.85M plus revolver availability of \$12.7M at June 30, 2024). That is a shortfall of about \$4.75M before considering the covenant, and about \$9.75M once the \$5M minimum-liquidity covenant is respected (somewhat less after one or two months of operating cash flow). The markup addresses the SEP piece by funding it in four \$500K installments at 90 days, 9, 15, and 21 months (Section 8.3; Comment 17). It leaves the FRC payment at 60 days, consistent with your instruction not to antagonize Andrade on fees. See Part VII, item 1.

## B. The 120% / 120-day counter does not, by itself, solve the problem

- 120% × \$10.8M = **\$12.96M**. That is more than the **\$12.7M** of revolver availability, so the email's statement that it is \"within the remaining capacity\" is not correct. It is also more than the **\$10M LC sub-limit** in the Beacon facility.

- The workbook's counter-proposal timeline shows \~\$3.89M of liquidity at month 4 and calls this \"tight but compliant.\" A \$3.89M figure is **below** the \$5M minimum-liquidity covenant, so the workbook's own numbers show a breach. (The underlying arithmetic, \$4.55M of cash less a \$0.26M negative revolver balance, also does not produce \$3.89M.)

- The email's alternative (50% at 120 days, balance at 180 days, all as LCs) also breaches. By month 6, cumulative outlays (FRC \$0.6M, penalty \$1.5M, SEP, FA \$12.96M) leave only about \$2.7M of liquidity with \$0.7M/month of operating cash flow, and about \$4.2M even if the SEP were paid in tranches.

- **Markup solution (Section 11.1; Comment 21):** 120% multiplier; \$6.48M (50% of \$12.96M) within 120 days; the balance recalculated at 120% of the cost of the Selected Remedies and posted within 60 days after CMS approval (outside date 21 months). This also lines up the financial assurance with the remedy decision. If MNA is selected at SWMU-3, the full amount is \$9.48M (within the LC sub-limit). If SWMU-4 is also allocated off-site, it is \$7.2M.

## C. GRS likely does not qualify for the RCRA financial test or a corporate guarantee

Your email and the workbook both treat the financial test or a corporate guarantee as the preferred mechanism. Measured against the criteria in 35 IAC 724.243(f) (40 C.F.R. § 264.143(f)(1)(i)), using the June 30, 2024 balance sheet (\$000s):

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Criterion (alternative I)**                       **Requirement**                                 **GRS (6/30/24)**                  **Result**
  --------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------- -----------------
  Total liabilities / net worth                       \< 2.0                                          60,500 / 24,200 = 2.50             Fails

  (Net income + D&A) / total liabilities              \> 0.10                                         (11,560 + 5,600) / 60,500 = 0.28   Passes

  Current assets / current liabilities                \> 1.5                                          29,000 / 45,200 = 0.64             Fails
